questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- If the file is outside the working directory, you must Read it in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: EnterWorktree
tools.description:
Use this tool ONLY when explicitly instructed to work in a worktree — either by the user directly, or by project instructions (CLAUDE.md / memory). This tool creates an isolated git worktree and switches the current session into it.

## When to Use

- The user explicitly says "worktree" (e.g., "start a worktree", "work in a worktree", "create a worktree", "use a worktree")
- CLAUDE.md or memory instructions direct you to work in a worktree for the current task

## When NOT to Use

- The user asks to create a branch, switch branches, or work on a different branch — use git commands instead
- The user asks to fix a bug or work on a feature — use normal git workflow unless worktrees are explicitly requested by the user or project instructions
- Never use this tool unless "worktree" is explicitly mentioned by the user or in CLAUDE.md / memory instructions

## Requirements

- Must be in a git repository, OR have WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks configured in settings.json
- Must not already be in a worktree session when creating a new worktree (`name`); switching into another existing worktree via `path` is allowed

## Behavior

- In a git repository: creates a new git worktree inside `.claude/worktrees/` on a new branch. The base ref is governed by the `worktree.baseRef` setting: `fresh` (default) branches from origin/<default-branch>; `head` branches from your current local HEAD
- Outside a git repository: delegates to WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks for VCS-agnostic isolation
- Switches the session's working directory to the new worktree
- Use ExitWorktree to leave the worktree mid-session (keep or remove). On session exit, if still in the worktree, the user will be prompted to keep or remove it

## Entering an existing worktree

Pass `path` instead of `name` to switch the session into a worktree that already exists (e.g., one you just created with `git worktree add`). On first entry from the launch directory, the path must appear in `git worktree list` for the repository that owns it — the current repository or, in a multi-repo workspace, a repository nested inside it; paths registered by neither are rejected. ExitWorktree will not remove a worktree entered this way; use `action: "keep"` to return to the original directory.

Switching with `path` also works when the session is already in a worktree (the previous worktree is left on disk, untouched, and only the new one is tracked for exit-time cleanup), and from agents whose working directory was pinned at launch (subagent isolation or explicit cwd). In both cases the target must be a worktree under `.claude/worktrees/` of the same repository, and from a pinned agent the switch only affects this agent, not the parent session. After a further switch, previously-visited worktrees are no longer writable — re-issue EnterWorktree with `path` to return to one.

## Parameters

- `name` (optional): A name for a new worktree. If neither `name` nor `path` is provided, a random name is generated.
- `path` (optional): Path to an existing worktree to enter instead of creating one — of the current repository, or (on first entry from the launch directory) of a repository nested inside it. Mutually exclusive with `name`.

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

A workflow size guideline is configured for this session: medium — keep workflows under 15 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

content.text:
**Short answer: neither is PFF. We use CFBD, plus a second EPA source called GameOnPaper.**

**What each source does:**
- **PFF:** We do not use PFF for EPA (expected points added) anywhere. PFF gives us the charting, blitz and coverage data, run concepts, and the Keys to Victory grades.
- **CFBD:** Gives the season-level EPA through its advanced stats. `matchup_pull.py` pulls it every Monday.
- **GameOnPaper:** Gives game-level EPA during and after a game. It uses ESPN's EPA model.

**One problem you should know about:**
- Your design note says to use **one EPA model only**, and it picks CFBD. GameOnPaper was to be a cross-check only. See `docs/epa-driven-tendency-method.md:45`.
- But your 9/13 review lists GameOnPaper as the EPA/play source in the reports. See `docs/advanced-stats-review-2026-09-13.md:15`.
- So in practice, the reports use two EPA models. The two models give different numbers for the same play.
- I did not check which source gave each EPA number in the Prairie View profile.

(Both docs are in `~/DEV/Football/MatchupAnalysis_FB2026/`.)

**You decide:**
1. **CFBD for all saved numbers. GameOnPaper only for live games.** CFBD cannot give live data on your plan, so you still need GameOnPaper during games. Postgame and season numbers all come from CFBD. **I recommend this one.** It matches the rule you already wrote.
2. **Keep both, but label the source on every EPA number.** This is less work now. But readers can still compare numbers from two different models.

I did not change any files.

**Short answer: No, I cannot get PFF's EPA. The PFF API does not give EPA.**

**What I checked:**
- All 4 PFF API spec files: no EPA field.
- The local PFF database (`pff.db`, 8 tables): no EPA column.
- The PFF play-call exports (49 columns): no EPA column.
- **Not checked:** the PFF Ultimate website. It may show an EPA number on some pages. Have you seen one there?

**Before we test, we must define "best."**
No source can tell us the "true" EPA for a play. So we cannot grade the sources against a right answer. For matchup work, "best" should mean this: **the EPA that predicts the next games best.** The tests below measure that.

**The 3 tests, cheapest first:**
1. **Agreement.** Do the sources give the same EPA per play for the same team and game? Where they do not agree, find the cause. Likely causes are garbage time, penalties, overtime, and FCS opponents.
2. **Stability.** Split each team's season into odd and even games. Does EPA in one half match EPA in the other half? More stable means less noise.
3. **Prediction.** Does EPA from games 1–6 predict the score margin in games 7–12? This is the only test that shows which source is "better." It needs all FBS teams, not only Baylor.

**Data we already have (no new CFBD calls):**
- CFBD EPA for every FBS game, 2019–2025, is cached in `~/DEV/CFB_Victory_Model/data/cfbd/advanced_game_*.csv`. That is enough for tests 2 and 3 on the CFBD side.
- Baylor plays, 2024–2025, are already joined to CFBD EPA in `~/DEV/PlayCalls_SuccessRate_EPA`. Your design note gave this join a week of work, but it is done.
- GameOnPaper must be scraped one game at a time. Baylor 2024–2025 is about 25 pages. All FBS teams would be about 1,500 pages, so tests 2 and 3 cost much more for GameOnPaper.

**Limits:**
- 2026 has only 2 games. All tests must use 2024–2025 data.
- If PFF shows EPA only on web pages, we can type in team totals by hand. We cannot get play-level PFF EPA. So PFF can join test 1 only.
- Your 9/13 review found that EPA "never changed a decision." So the answer may matter less than it seems. The test tells you if your "CFBD only" rule is correct.

**You decide:**
1. **Start small: test 1 on Baylor 2024–2025, CFBD vs GameOnPaper.** It costs about 25 page scrapes and no API calls. Do tests 2 and 3 only if the two sources do not agree. **I recommend this one.**
2. **Do all 3 tests on all FBS teams now.** This gives the real "which is best" answer. But GameOnPaper needs about 1,500 page scrapes.

Also tell me if you want me to check PFF Ultimate for an EPA number. I will only look, not change anything. I did not change any files.

# PFF API Reference (verified live 2026-09-06, field audit corrected 2026-09-07)

Account: `apikey@baylor.edu`, key stored in `~/DEV/Football/PFF_Data_Project/.env`
as `PFF_API_KEY`. Base URL `https://api.profootballfocus.com`. Never paste the key
into chat; read it from that file.

Answer to "do we have all the endpoints": yes for the four APIs with saved specs
(master data, grades, extended stats, premium) — 61 endpoints, all reachable and
returning 2026 data. The key also carries permissions for `a22`, `iq`,
`open_exchange`, `player_tracking`, `translations`, and `video`, but no OpenAPI
spec for those is saved locally and the docs portal (`/doc`) sits behind a browser
login, so those paths are unknown.

## READ FIRST: PFF omits zero-valued fields

**A field appears on a row only when its value is non-zero.** Enumerating a feed's
schema from `rows[0].keys()` silently misses most of the interesting fields. This
caused a wrong conclusion on 2026-09-07 ("PFF has no turnover or scoring data") that
took a full re-audit to catch.

Measured on game 31098:

| Feed | keys in row 0 | keys anywhere | missed |
|---|---|---|---|
| `passing` | 62 | **87** | 25 |
| `team_main` | 32 | **93** | 61 |
| `team_play` | 26 | **45** | 19 |
| `rushing` | 49 | 58 | 9 |
| `game_grade` | 17 | 40 | 23 |

Always enumerate as a union:

```python
keys = set()
for r in rows: keys |= set(r)
```

The saved OpenAPI specs in `docs/swagger/` are the authoritative field list, not any
sample response. `docs/swagger/locate.py` maps schema fields to endpoints.

import yaml, os, glob, collections

TARGET = ["interception","fumble","touchdown","turnover","points","score",

def walk(node, path, out, depth=0):
    if depth>12: return
    if isinstance(node, dict):
        for k,v in node.items():

                        typ = (pdef or {}).get("type") if isinstance(pdef,dict) else None

entries.description:
Use a mouse and keyboard to interact with a web browser, and take screenshots. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.
* Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element before moving the cursor.
* If you tried clicking on a program or link but it failed to load, even after waiting, try adjusting your click location so that the tip of the cursor visually falls on the element that you want to click.
* Make sure to click any buttons, links, icons, etc with the cursor tip in the center of the element. Don't click boxes on their edges unless asked.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported and will return an error - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Title: PFF API Documentation
URL: https://api.profootballfocus.com/doc
Source element: <article>
---
Pro Football Focus API User Guide
Getting Started

Access to PFF APIs is available exclusively to our B2B clients. If you are a PFF B2B customer and need an API key, please contact our Service team to request one. API keys are not available to the general public.

All PFF APIs are available at the https://:api.profootballfocus.com endpoint. Note that this is an https endpoint rather than http, you should not communicate with our APIs over http.

Documentation for the PFF APIs is available in an OpenAPI Specification (Swagger). Please consult the documentation, if you come across something that is wrong, isn't clear or needs further detail then please contact us and we'll be happy to incorporate your feedback.

Basic Usage

To use a PFF API you must first exchange your API key for a JWT token. You can then use this token to make subsequent API calls. Using your API key submit a POST request to the PFF API login endpoint including your API key as a x-api-key request header. The response to this request should be a JSON object that includes a JWT token. Using that JWT token in the Bearer Authorization header in a subsequent response will enable you to access our APIs.

This process is perhaps best explained with a simple example using a command line approach with curl:

Step 1 - Exchange your API key for a JSON Web Token (JWT)
$ curl -X POST -H "x-api-key: C88B277B-D33C-4FBB-8FA3-1CF761A40EAA" \
https://api.profootballfocus.com/auth/login

Assuming the request is structured correctly and the API key is valid, this request will return a JSON response that includes the JWT token, for example:

{"jwt":"eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJpc3MiOiJQRkYuSG9kb3IiLCJpYXQiOjE1NTc0MzAwNjgsImV4cCI6MTU4ODk2NjA2OCwiYXVkIjoiUEZGLkhvZG9yIiwic3ViIjoibmVpbC1sb3Zlcy1nbGl0dGVyQGV4YW1wbGUuY29tIiwiR2l2ZW5OYW1lIjoiSm9obm55IiwiU3VybmFtZSI6IlJvY2tldCIsIkVtYWlsIjoianJvY2tldEBleGFtcGxlLmNvbSIsIlJvbGUiOlsiTWFuYWdlciIsIlByb2plY3QgQWRtaW5pc3RyYXRvciJdfQ.yIWyUGbt1-IMPZIWH3z6DuZ4hh5Z0vdjypPahKEY1MU"}

In the event that your authorization step fails you will receive a 401 - Unauthorized response with the following response body {"errors": {"detail": "Unauthorized"}}

On successful authorization copy the JWT token value to your clipboard and export it as an environment variable for use later:

$ export JWT=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJpc3MiOiJQRkYuSG9kb3IiLCJpYXQiOjE1NTc0MzAwNjgsImV4cCI6MTU4ODk2NjA2OCwiYXVkIjoiUEZGLkhvZG9yIiwic3ViIjoibmVpbC1sb3Zlcy1nbGl0dGVyQGV4YW1wbGUuY29tIiwiR2l2ZW5OYW1lIjoiSm9obm55IiwiU3VybmFtZSI6IlJvY2tldCIsIkVtYWlsIjoianJvY2tldEBleGFtcGxlLmNvbSIsIlJvbGUiOlsiTWFuYWdlciIsIlByb2plY3QgQWRtaW5pc3RyYXRvciJdfQ.yIWyUGbt1-IMPZIWH3z6DuZ4hh5Z0vdjypPahKEY1MU
Step 2 - Use the JWT token to access our APIs

Once you've obtained a JWT token using the above steps, you can use it to access PFF APIs by setting the request header of a subsequent HTTP request. The request header must be of the form Authorization: Bearer ${JWT}, as illustrated by the following curl example:

$ curl -H "Authorization: Bearer ${JWT}" -v \
https://api.profootballfocus.com/v1/video/nfl/games/9312/offense
API Usage Guidelines
The JWT token has a limited life

The API Key is only used in an Authorization call to exchange it for a token which is used to make subsequent calls to all other APIs. The token returned from the authentication call is valid for a limited amount of time. You will need to periodically obtain a new token by calling the auth login API with your API Key as per Step 1 above. Your code should also handle an HTTP 401 indicating that the token you are using is no longer valid.

API calls are rate limited

API calls are rate limited both globally and for a specific token. This is intended to protect the availability of the overall system for all users. Your code that calls the API should handle an HTTP 429 response for rate limited calls. In the event that your requests are rate limited will receive a 429 - Too Many Requests response with the following response body {"errors": {"detail": "Too many requests"}}. Your code should handle rate limiting.

Access to APIs is controlled through permissions

We control access to specific APIs through a permissions system. If you need access to an API that you currently can't access, please contact us to request access.

Access to data by league is controlled through permissions

You should be able to access data from any league that you have purchased. If you believe you have purchased data for a particular league and still cannot access it via the APIs then please contact us so we can check your permissions.

Some API responses are large and use HTTP chunked transfer encoding

Some of the API responses - particularly those for season long extracts - can be very large. In these cases, the response is sent using HTTP chunked transfer encoding. It is therefore necessary to use an API client that is capable of consuming such chunked responses. While many API client tools and libraries exist that support chunked transfer encoding, the popular Postman tool is a notable exception, and therefore Postman cannot be used for accessing all of the PFF APIs. On the other hand, the cURL tool used for the examples in this document does support chunked transfers. Note that, currently, the Master Data APIs do not use chunked transfer encoding so it is possible to use Postman for accessing the Master Data APIs.

It is also possible to request that the response data be transferred in compressed form, which can result in significantly faster responses. The HTTP response header Content-Encoding: gzip will be set on the response whenever the response data is compressed.

To indicate that the client can accept and handle compressed data, set the HTTP request header Accept-Encoding to the value gzip, as per the following example:

$ curl -H "Authorization: Bearer ${JWT}" -H "Accept-Encoding: gzip" \
--compressed -v -o ncaa_2017_defense.json \
'https://api.profootballfocus.com/v1/analytics/projections/ncaa/2017/defense'

(The --compressed option instructs curl to expect compressed response data and decompress it when saving to disk.)

API Reference

The PFF APIs are documented using an OpenAPI specification (formerly known as Swagger).

Reference documentation for all of the available PFF APIs is available at the links below. Access to this documentation is restricted to those individuals with Ultimate access, if you cannot access the documentation using your Ultimate credentials and would like access please contact our Service team.

PFF Bearer Auth: API for obtaining a Bearer auth token
PFF Master Data: API for accessing various data about franchises, leagues, teams, players, etc.
PFF Video Feeds: API for accessing video feeds
PFF A22 Feeds: API for accessing a22 feeds
PFF Play Diagrams: API for accessing play diagrams
Premium Feeds: API for accessing feeds to replace most used PSV1 feeds
PFF Translations Feeds: API for accessing translations feeds
PFF Extended Stats Feeds: API for accessing various extended player stats by game
Player Tracking Feeds: Player tracking API feeds
Grades Feeds: API for accessing grades feeds to replace PSV1 feeds.
Open Exchange Feeds: API for freely available data fields.
IQ Feeds: API for accessing IQ feeds.
Not seeing the documentation links that you expect to see?

You might be logged in as a user that does not have permission to view the documentation for a particular API. If so, you can click the Logout button to logout and then login as a different user.

LOGOUT

import json, re, requests
from dotenv import dotenv_values
key = dotenv_values(".env").get("PFF_API_KEY","").strip()
B = "https://api.profootballfocus.com"; UA = {"User-Agent":"Mozilla/5.0","Accept-Encoding":"gzip"}
jwt = requests.post(B+"/auth/login", headers={**UA,"x-api-key":key}, timeout=30).json()["jwt"]
H = {**UA, "Authorization":"Bearer "+jwt}
s = requests.get(B+"/doc/swagger/iq-feeds.yaml", headers=H, timeout=30, allow_redirects=False)
print("spec via JWT:", s.status_code, s.headers.get("content-type"), len(s.text))
r = requests.get(B+"/v1/iq/ncaa/games/31098/win_probability", headers=H, timeout=60)
print("win_probability 31098:", r.status_code, len(r.content), "bytes")
if r.ok:
    d = r.json()
    rows = next((v for v in d.values() if isinstance(v, list)), d if isinstance(d, list) else [])
    print("top keys:", list(d)[:10] if isinstance(d, dict) else "list", "rows:", len(rows))
    keys = set()
    for row in rows: keys |= set(row)
    print("all fields:", sorted(keys))
    hits = sorted(k for k in keys if re.search(r"ep|expect|point|wp|win|prob", k, re.I))
    print("EP/WP-like:", hits)
    for k in hits[:8]:
        vals = [row[k] for row in rows if k in row][:5]
        print(f"  {k}: n={sum(k in row for row in rows)} sample={vals}")
else:
    print(r.text[:200])
EOF

import re, json, requests, duckdb, statistics as st
from dotenv import dotenv_values
c = duckdb.connect("data/pff.db", read_only=True)
cols = [r[0] for r in c.execute("select column_name from information_schema.columns where table_name='games'").fetchall()]
print("games cols:", cols[:30])
sc = next((x for x in cols if x in ("season","season_id","year")), None)
where = " or ".join(f"cast({x} as varchar)='118'" for x in cols if re.search(r"franchise|team_id", x))
q = f"select * from games where ({where})" + (f" and cast({sc} as varchar) like '%2025%'" if sc else "") + " limit 3"
try:
    g = c.execute(q).fetchdf(); print(g.iloc[:, :10].to_string()); g25 = int(g.iloc[0][[x for x in cols if x in ("id","game_id")][0]])
except Exception as e:
    print("lookup failed:", e); g25 = None
key = dotenv_values(".env").get("PFF_API_KEY","").strip()
B="https://api.profootballfocus.com"; UA={"User-Agent":"Mozilla/5.0","Accept-Encoding":"gzip"}
jwt = requests.post(B+"/auth/login", headers={**UA,"x-api-key":key}, timeout=30).json()["jwt"]
H={**UA,"Authorization":"Bearer "+jwt}
EP=("expected_points","expected_points_added","expected_points_legacy","expected_points_added_legacy")
for gid in [31098] + ([g25] if g25 else []):
    r = requests.get(f"{B}/v1/video/ncaa/games/{gid}/plays", headers=H, timeout=90)
    print(f"\n/plays game {gid}: HTTP {r.status_code} {len(r.content)} bytes")
    if not r.ok: print(r.text[:200]); continue
    d=r.json(); rows=next((v for v in d.values() if isinstance(v,list)),[])
    print(" rows:", len(rows))
    for k in EP:
        v=[x[k] for x in rows if x.get(k) is not None]
        print(f"  {k}: n={len(v)}/{len(rows)}" + (f" mean={st.mean(v):.3f} sum={sum(v):.1f} range=[{min(v):.2f},{max(v):.2f}]" if v else ""))
    same = sum(1 for x in rows if x.get("expected_points_added") is not None and x.get("expected_points_added")==x.get("expected_points_added_legacy"))
    print("  EPA == legacy on", same, "plays")
    keys=set()
    for x in rows: keys|=set(x)
    print("  join fields:", sorted(k for k in keys if re.search(r"^(quarter|clock|game_clock|down|distance|field_position|yards?_to_go|offense|defense|play_type|run_pass|score|gsis|teamworks|play_id|game_id|penalty|no_play)", k))[:30])
EOF

# PFF Data Project — Agent Guide

This file is the canonical project memory for any AI coding agent working in this
repo. It is mirrored verbatim into `AGENTS.md` so OpenAI Codex (and any other
agent that reads `AGENTS.md`) gets the same context. A pre-commit hook in
`.githooks/pre-commit` blocks commits where the two files diverge.

If you edit one, edit both. See "Keeping CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md in sync" below.

---

## What this project is

A standalone Python data pipeline that pulls Pro Football Focus (PFF) game and
player data into a local **DuckDB** database for Baylor University Football
analysis. Scope is **Baylor + every Big 12 team + non-conference opponents** for
the **current season plus two prior**.

The DB *is* the deliverable. There are no dashboards in this repo. Downstream
consumers — Power BI, Jupyter notebooks, and a future athlete management system
(AMS) project that will unify PFF with Catapult GPS, VALD ForceDecks, and Perch
VBT data — own visualization and cross-domain joins.

## Sister pipelines (do not modify from here)

- **VALD ForceDecks (CMJ/IMTP):** `..\..\ForcePlate_DecisionSystem` — the
  architectural template this project mirrors.
- **Catapult GPS:** `..\..\DataBase_GPS_Reporting`
- **Perch VBT:** not yet built.

The pattern across all of them is: per-domain Python pipeline → per-domain DB →
future AMS layer unions them on `(athlete_id, source_system, pulled_at)`.

## Tech stack

- Python 3.12+
- `duckdb`, `requests`, `python-dotenv`, `PyJWT`, `pyyaml`, `pandas`, `pytest`
- No web framework, no ORM, no dashboard libs — keep it lean

## Layout

```
PFF_Data_Project/
├── CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md       # this file (mirrored)
├── README.md                   # user-facing setup and usage
├── requirements.txt
├── .env.example                # PFF_BASE_URL, PFF_API_KEY, BAYLOR_TEAM_ID
├── .gitignore
├── .githooks/pre-commit        # blocks CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md divergence
├── run_pipeline.py             # CLI entry
├── config/
│   └── pipeline.yaml           # team/season scope, endpoints, retry config
├── src/
│   ├── db.py                   # DuckDB schema + connect + backup helpers
│   ├── ingest/
│   │   ├── pff_client.py       # PFF HTTP client (stub until Phase 0 done)
│   │   └── pipeline.py         # Orchestration: dims → facts → log
│   └── shape/transform.py      # JSON → tidy rows (teams/games/grades/stats/premium)
├── data/                       # DuckDB lives here (gitignored)
├── docs/
│   └── pff_api_notes.md        # Phase 0 spike output
├── scripts/
│   └── phase0_probe.py         # Credential discovery probe
└── tests/
    ├── test_db.py
    └── fixtures/
```

## Data model contract

Dimensions are stable identities; facts are timestamped measurements.

- **Dimensions:** `teams`, `players`, `player_seasons`, `games`
- **Facts:** `pff_grades` (per-player per-game, long form), `pff_stats` (extended
  stats, long form), `pff_premium` (advanced metrics, keyed JSON passthrough)
- **Operational:** `ingest_log`

`players` / `player_seasons` are derived from the grade rows (which carry
player_id, name, position, team_id, season) — cleanest "who actually played"
source; avoids the giant all-NCAA `/players` pull.

Every fact row carries `source_system = 'PFF'` and `pulled_at`. This is
non-negotiable — it is the contract the future AMS layer relies on to union PFF
with Catapult, VALD, and Perch facts.

`pff_player_id` is the durable join key. This pipeline does **not** maintain a
canonical athlete master record across systems. That mapping
(`roster.athlete_id → pff_player_id`) belongs to the future AMS project. Do not
invent it here.

## API contract (Phase 0 complete)

Full contract is in `docs/pff_api_notes.md`; OpenAPI specs in `docs/swagger/`.
Essentials:

- **Auth:** `POST /auth/login` with header `x-api-key: <key>` → `{"jwt"}`. Send
  `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>` on all calls. JWT lasts ~1h; re-auth on 401.
  Rate-limited (HTTP 429) — client backs off. `src/ingest/pff_client.py` owns this.
- **Base:** `https://api.profootballfocus.com`, league slug `ncaa`, season = year.
- **Baylor:** team_id / franchise_id = `118` (`BAYLOR_TEAM_ID` in `.env`).
- **Scope is open:** the key reads all NCAA teams + grades for any game, so
  Baylor + Big 12 + opponents is achievable despite the token's `franchise:118`
  constraint.
- **No raw play-by-play.** Premium feeds (`/v1/premium/...`) provide play-level
  advanced metrics → captured in `pff_premium` as keyed JSON passthrough.
- **FUTURE:** player-tracking feeds are deliberately not modeled in v1.

## Conventions

- **Credentials never in code.** `.env` only. Loaded via `python-dotenv`. The
  `.env` file is gitignored; `.env.example` is committed as the template.
- **DuckDB upserts:** use `INSERT OR REPLACE INTO` (idempotent refresh — re-pulling
  a week updates values rather than duplicating). See `_upsert` in `pipeline.py`.
- **Config path resolution:** always anchor to `Path(__file__).resolve().parent`
  walks, never relative paths from CWD. `run_pipeline.py` and `src/db.py` show
  the pattern.
- **Backups before destructive ops:** copy `data/pff.db` to
  `data/pff_before_<operation>_<YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS>.db` first.
  `src/db.backup_db()` does this — use it from any new destructive code path.
- **Idempotent ingests:** running the same week twice must be a no-op.
- **One concern per module.** Client does HTTP. Shape does JSON-to-rows. Pipeline
  orchestrates. db.py owns the schema. Don't blur these.
- **Tests use mocked HTTP**, not live API calls. The Phase 0 probe is the only
  script that hits the real API.
- **No comments that narrate the obvious.** Comments are for non-obvious WHYs
  (e.g., "DuckDB requires ON CONFLICT here; SQLite syntax silently fails").

## CLI commands

```
python run_pipeline.py --dry-run               # auth + scope check, no writes
python run_pipeline.py --backfill              # full 3-season pull
python run_pipeline.py --season 2025           # full season
python run_pipeline.py --season 2025 --week 8  # one week
python run_pipeline.py --diagnose [NAME]       # query local DB
python run_pipeline.py --reset-db              # backup + reinit
```

## Testing

```
pytest tests/
```

Tests that need a DB use a per-test temp path; don't touch `data/pff.db`.

## Keeping CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md in sync

`AGENTS.md` is a byte-identical copy of `CLAUDE.md`. The pre-commit hook at
`.githooks/pre-commit` blocks commits when they differ. Activate the hook once
per clone:

```
git config core.hooksPath .githooks
```

When updating agent guidance, edit `CLAUDE.md` first, then:

```
cp CLAUDE.md AGENTS.md
git add CLAUDE.md AGENTS.md
```

If you intentionally need them to diverge (tool-specific instructions for one
agent), update the hook before committing — don't bypass it silently with
`--no-verify`.

## Working with this repo from Codex

Codex reads `AGENTS.md` automatically. Everything above applies to Codex
sessions identically. Codex-specific notes, if any are ever needed, go in a
separate section here and get mirrored.


## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

  `score`, `penalty`, `no_play`, `gsis_play_id`.

- IQ `/v1/iq/ncaa/games/{game_id}/win_probability` has per-play win probability
  (`current_wp`, `post_play`) and go-for-it calls. No expected points.

# PFF API Reference (verified live 2026-09-06)

Account: `apikey@baylor.edu`, key stored in `~/DEV/Football/PFF_Data_Project/.env`
as `PFF_API_KEY`. Base URL `https://api.profootballfocus.com`. Never paste the key
into chat; read it from that file.

Answer to "do we have all the endpoints": yes for the four APIs with saved specs
(master data, grades, extended stats, premium) — 61 endpoints, all reachable and
returning 2026 data. The key also carries permissions for `a22`, `iq`,
`open_exchange`, `player_tracking`, `translations`, and `video`, but no OpenAPI
spec for those is saved locally and the docs portal (`/doc`) sits behind a browser
login, so those paths are unknown.

## Auth

1. `POST /auth/login` with header `x-api-key: <key>` returns `{"jwt": "..."}`
2. Send `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>` on every call
3. JWT lives 3600s. On `401 {"errors":{"detail":"Unauthorized"}}`, re-auth.
4. `429 {"errors":{"detail":"Too many requests"}}` is real. Back off exponentially.
5. Health check, no auth: `GET /status` returns `"Hodor"`

**Gotcha:** the default Python urllib user agent gets a `403` at the edge. Use
curl (or set a browser User-Agent on requests). Same trap as ESPN.

Send `Accept-Encoding: gzip` / curl `--compressed`; season feeds are large.

## Identifiers

- League slug: `ncaa` (also `nfl`, `ufl`, `aaf` on this key)
- Season: integer year, e.g. `2026`
- Baylor: `team_id` 118, `franchise_id` 118, abbreviation `BAYLOR`. Not to be
  confused with Mary Hardin-Baylor, id 1245.
- Games are keyed home/away by `franchise_id`, not `team_id`
- `gsis_id` on a game row is the ESPN game id, which is the join key to
  GameOnPaper and the CFBD work
- Token carries `constraints.franchise:["118"]` but this does not restrict reads.
  All 958 NCAA teams and every opponent game come back fine.

## Master Data (15 endpoints)

| Path | Returns |
|---|---|
| `GET /v1/leagues` | leagues (NFL=1, NCAA=2, UFL=6) |
| `GET /v1/{league}/{season}/teams` | teams (958 for NCAA 2026); conference is in `groups[]` |
| `GET /v1/{league}/{season}/games` | games (1,614 for NCAA 2026, weeks 0-13 and 15) |
| `GET /v1/{league}/players` | players; `page`, `page_size` |
| `GET /v1/{league}/players/latest` | latest snapshot; `q`, `id`, `sort`, `dir`, `updated_since` |
| `GET /v1/{league}/players/export` | bulk player CSV |
| `GET /v1/{league}/franchises` | franchises |
| `GET /v1/{league}/franchises/{franchise_id}/team_members` | roster; `effective_date` |
| `GET /v1/{league}/franchises/{franchise_id}/package_depth_charts` | depth chart by package; `active` |
| `GET /v1/{league}/depth_charts` | all depth charts (25,732 rows NCAA) |
| `GET /v1/{league}/injuries` | injury detail (7,228 rows) |
| `GET /v1/{league}/game_status` | game availability (4,874 rows) |
| `GET /v1/{league}/practice_status` | practice status (229 rows) |
| `GET /v1/player_combine_results` | combine; `player_id` |
| `GET /v1/player_pro_day` | pro day; `player_id` |

## Grades (12 endpoints)

Per game:
- `GET /v1/grades/{league}/games/{game_id}/game_grade` — per player per game
- `GET /v1/grades/{league}/games/{game_id}/team_game_grades`
- `GET /v1/grades/{league}/games/{game_id}/special_team_game_grade`

Per season:
- `GET /v1/grades/{league}/{season}/game_grade` — every player game grade
- `GET /v1/grades/{league}/{season}/special_team_game_grade`
- `GET /v1/grades/{league}/{season}/season_grade` (27,333 rows for 2026)
- `GET /v1/grades/{league}/{season}/special_team_season_grade`
- `GET /v1/grades/{league}/{season}/career_grade`
- `GET /v1/grades/{league}/{season}/team_season_grades`
- `GET /v1/grades/{league}/{season}/team_game_grades`

Season to date by week:
- `GET /v1/grades/{league}/{season_id}/{week_id}/season_grade`
- `GET /v1/grades/{league}/{season_id}/{week_id}/special_team_season_grade`

All accept `?format=`. Grade rows are wide: `overall`, `offense`, `defense`,
`coverage`, `pass_rush`, `run_defense`, `discipline`, matching `*_snaps` and
`*_rank` columns, keyed by `player_id`, `unit`, `position`, `team_id`, `game_id`.
Melt to long form before storing.

## Premium (22 endpoints) — this is the play-by-play

Correction to the old Phase 0 note: premium feeds are **not** aggregated
season stats. They are play-level and player-play-level, with PFF's charting tags.
This is the layer that matters for tendency work.

Per game: `GET /v1/premium/{league}/games/{game_id}/{category}`
Per season: `GET /v1/premium/{league}/{season}/{category}`

| Category | Grain | What is in it |
|---|---|---|
| `team_play` | one row per play | down, distance, field position, quarter, clock, offense/defense, `shotgun`, `pistol`, `play_action`, `no_huddle`, `screen`, `draw`, `trick`, `trick_look`, `shift`, `pre_kick_motion`, `pump_fake`, `redzone`, personnel counts |
| `team_main` | one row per player per play | `role`, `position`, `motion`, `on_los`, `bunched`, `creeper`, `def_coverage`, `def_pass_rush`, `off_pass_route`, `off_run_block`, `off_pass_block`, per-play grades by phase |
| `passing` | one row per dropback | `route`, `pass_depth`, `pass_direction`, `coverage_scheme`, `coverage_name`, `mofo_coverage_shown` vs `mofo_coverage_played`, `off_package`, `def_package`, `time_to_throw`, `big_time_throw`, `turnover_worthy_play`, `yards_after_catch` |
| `pressure` | one row per pressure | rusher and blocker identity, `blitz`, `tech`, `shade`, `stance`, `dropback_type`, `time_to_throw_group` |
| `pass_rush` | one row per rusher per dropback | alignment `tech`/`shade`/`side`, `defensive_backs` count, `third_down_group` |
| `pass_protection` | pass-pro assignments | blocker side |
| `all_blocking` | one row per block | `block_type`, blocked player and technique, `missed_assignment`, `unblocked`, `cut`, `looper`, `spy` |
| `quarterback_charting` | one row per attempt | `pass_accuracy`, `throw_type`, `qb_look`, `rhythm`, `quick_game`, `receiver_separation`, `hit_while_throwing`, `coverage_type` |
| `rushing` | rush detail | |
| `penalty` | penalty detail | |
| `team_analysis` | play-level notes and ratings | `rps` (run/pass/special), `comment` |

Volume reference, one 2025 Baylor game (id 28762): team_play 180, team_main 3,960,
all_blocking 1,838, pass_rush 355, pressure 115, passing 86, qb_charting 85,
team_analysis 394. Season-level 2026 `team_play` is 33,553 rows and climbing.

## Extended Stats (10 endpoints)

`GET /v1/stats/extended/{league}/{season}/{category}`, optional `player_id`.
Categories: `offense`, `defense`, `receiving`, `rushing`, `special`, `kickoff`,
`kickret`, `punt`, `puntret`, `penalty`. Grain is player by game.
2026 offense returned 7,688 rows.

## Data availability and lag (checked 2026-09-06)

- Grades post first. Baylor at Auburn (game 31098, played 9/5) already had 116
  game_grade rows the next morning.
- Premium lags grades. That same game returned 0 premium rows; week 0 and the
  9/3 week 1 games were fully populated. Expect roughly one to three days.
- A `200` with an empty array means not processed yet, not an error. Always check
  row count before treating a pull as complete.
- 2025 and prior seasons are complete and safe to backfill.

## Pagination

Season collections return in full with no pagination (958 teams, 1,614 games,
33k plays in one response). Only `/v1/{league}/players` documents `page` and
`page_size`. Don't assume paging elsewhere, but assert row counts.

## Baylor 2026 game ids

| Wk | Game id | Date (UTC) | ESPN id |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 31098 | 2026-09-05 | 411396 |
| 2 | 31122 | 2026-09-13 | 411504 |
| 3 | 31257 | 2026-09-19 | 411571 |
| 4 | 31278 | 2026-09-26 | 411683 |
| 5 | 31348 | 2026-10-03 | 411698 |

Twelve games total. Pull the full list from `/v1/ncaa/2026/games` filtered on
`franchise_id` 118.

## Where PFF fits next to the other sources

- CFBD: free tier, 1,000 calls a month, no live endpoints. Historical and
  season context only.
- GameOnPaper: live EPA and win probability, scraped, no auth.
- PFF: the only source here with charted formation, coverage, alignment, and
  pass-rush tags. Use it for tendencies, not for live in-game.
- Join on `gsis_id` (game) which is the ESPN game id used by the other two.

## Existing code

`~/DEV/Football/PFF_Data_Project/` — `src/ingest/pff_client.py`, `run_pipeline.py`,
`scripts/phase0_probe.py`, SQLite at `data/pff.db`. Specs in `docs/swagger/`.

# PFF Data Project — Agent Guide

This file is the canonical project memory for any AI coding agent working in this
repo. It is mirrored verbatim into `AGENTS.md` so OpenAI Codex (and any other
agent that reads `AGENTS.md`) gets the same context. A pre-commit hook in
`.githooks/pre-commit` blocks commits where the two files diverge.

If you edit one, edit both. See "Keeping CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md in sync" below.

---

## What this project is

A standalone Python data pipeline that pulls Pro Football Focus (PFF) game and
player data into a local **DuckDB** database for Baylor University Football
analysis. Scope is **Baylor + every Big 12 team + non-conference opponents** for
the **current season plus two prior**.

The DB *is* the deliverable. There are no dashboards in this repo. Downstream
consumers — Power BI, Jupyter notebooks, and a future athlete management system
(AMS) project that will unify PFF with Catapult GPS, VALD ForceDecks, and Perch
VBT data — own visualization and cross-domain joins.

## Sister pipelines (do not modify from here)

- **VALD ForceDecks (CMJ/IMTP):** `..\..\ForcePlate_DecisionSystem` — the
  architectural template this project mirrors.
- **Catapult GPS:** `..\..\DataBase_GPS_Reporting`
- **Perch VBT:** not yet built.

The pattern across all of them is: per-domain Python pipeline → per-domain DB →
future AMS layer unions them on `(athlete_id, source_system, pulled_at)`.

## Tech stack

- Python 3.12+
- `duckdb`, `requests`, `python-dotenv`, `PyJWT`, `pyyaml`, `pandas`, `pytest`
- No web framework, no ORM, no dashboard libs — keep it lean

## Layout

```
PFF_Data_Project/
├── CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md       # this file (mirrored)
├── README.md                   # user-facing setup and usage
├── requirements.txt
├── .env.example                # PFF_BASE_URL, PFF_API_KEY, BAYLOR_TEAM_ID
├── .gitignore
├── .githooks/pre-commit        # blocks CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md divergence
├── run_pipeline.py             # CLI entry
├── config/
│   └── pipeline.yaml           # team/season scope, endpoints, retry config
├── src/
│   ├── db.py                   # DuckDB schema + connect + backup helpers
│   ├── ingest/
│   │   ├── pff_client.py       # PFF HTTP client (stub until Phase 0 done)
│   │   └── pipeline.py         # Orchestration: dims → facts → log
│   └── shape/transform.py      # JSON → tidy rows (teams/games/grades/stats/premium)
├── data/                       # DuckDB lives here (gitignored)
├── docs/
│   └── pff_api_notes.md        # Phase 0 spike output
├── scripts/
│   └── phase0_probe.py         # Credential discovery probe
└── tests/
    ├── test_db.py
    └── fixtures/
```

## Data model contract

Dimensions are stable identities; facts are timestamped measurements.

- **Dimensions:** `teams`, `players`, `player_seasons`, `games`
- **Facts:** `pff_grades` (per-player per-game, long form), `pff_stats` (extended
  stats, long form), `pff_premium` (advanced metrics, keyed JSON passthrough)
- **Operational:** `ingest_log`

`players` / `player_seasons` are derived from the grade rows (which carry
player_id, name, position, team_id, season) — cleanest "who actually played"
source; avoids the giant all-NCAA `/players` pull.

Every fact row carries `source_system = 'PFF'` and `pulled_at`. This is
non-negotiable — it is the contract the future AMS layer relies on to union PFF
with Catapult, VALD, and Perch facts.

`pff_player_id` is the durable join key. This pipeline does **not** maintain a
canonical athlete master record across systems. That mapping
(`roster.athlete_id → pff_player_id`) belongs to the future AMS project. Do not
invent it here.

## API contract (Phase 0 complete)

Full contract is in `docs/pff_api_notes.md`; OpenAPI specs in `docs/swagger/`.
Essentials:

- **Auth:** `POST /auth/login` with header `x-api-key: <key>` → `{"jwt"}`. Send
  `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>` on all calls. JWT lasts ~1h; re-auth on 401.
  Rate-limited (HTTP 429) — client backs off. `src/ingest/pff_client.py` owns this.
- **Base:** `https://api.profootballfocus.com`, league slug `ncaa`, season = year.
- **Baylor:** team_id / franchise_id = `118` (`BAYLOR_TEAM_ID` in `.env`).
- **Scope is open:** the key reads all NCAA teams + grades for any game, so
  Baylor + Big 12 + opponents is achievable despite the token's `franchise:118`
  constraint.
- **No raw play-by-play.** Premium feeds (`/v1/premium/...`) provide play-level
  advanced metrics → captured in `pff_premium` as keyed JSON passthrough.
- **FUTURE:** player-tracking feeds are deliberately not modeled in v1.

## Conventions

- **Credentials never in code.** `.env` only. Loaded via `python-dotenv`. The
  `.env` file is gitignored; `.env.example` is committed as the template.
- **DuckDB upserts:** use `INSERT OR REPLACE INTO` (idempotent refresh — re-pulling
  a week updates values rather than duplicating). See `_upsert` in `pipeline.py`.
- **Config path resolution:** always anchor to `Path(__file__).resolve().parent`
  walks, never relative paths from CWD. `run_pipeline.py` and `src/db.py` show
  the pattern.
- **Backups before destructive ops:** copy `data/pff.db` to
  `data/pff_before_<operation>_<YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS>.db` first.
  `src/db.backup_db()` does this — use it from any new destructive code path.
- **Idempotent ingests:** running the same week twice must be a no-op.
- **One concern per module.** Client does HTTP. Shape does JSON-to-rows. Pipeline
  orchestrates. db.py owns the schema. Don't blur these.
- **Tests use mocked HTTP**, not live API calls. The Phase 0 probe is the only
  script that hits the real API.
- **No comments that narrate the obvious.** Comments are for non-obvious WHYs
  (e.g., "DuckDB requires ON CONFLICT here; SQLite syntax silently fails").

## CLI commands

```
python run_pipeline.py --dry-run               # auth + scope check, no writes
python run_pipeline.py --backfill              # full 3-season pull
python run_pipeline.py --season 2025           # full season
python run_pipeline.py --season 2025 --week 8  # one week
python run_pipeline.py --diagnose [NAME]       # query local DB
python run_pipeline.py --reset-db              # backup + reinit
```

## Testing

```
pytest tests/
```

Tests that need a DB use a per-test temp path; don't touch `data/pff.db`.

## Keeping CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md in sync

`AGENTS.md` is a byte-identical copy of `CLAUDE.md`. The pre-commit hook at
`.githooks/pre-commit` blocks commits when they differ. Activate the hook once
per clone:

```
git config core.hooksPath .githooks
```

When updating agent guidance, edit `CLAUDE.md` first, then:

```
cp CLAUDE.md AGENTS.md
git add CLAUDE.md AGENTS.md
```

If you intentionally need them to diverge (tool-specific instructions for one
agent), update the hook before committing — don't bypass it silently with
`--no-verify`.

## Working with this repo from Codex

Codex reads `AGENTS.md` automatically. Everything above applies to Codex
sessions identically. Codex-specific notes, if any are ever needed, go in a
separate section here and get mirrored.


## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

# MatchupAnalysis_FB2026

Week-by-week opponent matchup analysis for Baylor football, 2026 season. Identify
tendencies, project outcomes, and grade the Keys to Victory off PFF.

**This folder is the source of truth for the project.** Claude Code reads it natively.
Cowork sessions read it once the folder is connected. Nothing about this project should
live only in a cloud project doc, a chat, or someone's memory.

## Read first

| Doc | When |
|---|---|
| `docs/working-conventions.md` | Always. Where output goes, what the core sources are. |
| `docs/weekly-routine.md` | The Monday and Thursday scheduled runs, the collection script, the two-game rule, the CFBD budget guard. |
| `docs/data-access.md` | Credentials, CFBD limits and traps, GameOnPaper scraping, the three-layer source split. |
| `docs/coordinator-continuity.md` | Whose 2025 tape predicts which side of the ball. Read before any 2025-basis profile. |

## Reference

- `docs/pff-api-reference.md` — 61 verified endpoints, the sparse-field trap, auth, identifiers, Baylor 2026 game ids
- `docs/keys-framework.md` — Keys to Victory v3 and the auto-grader
- `docs/load-per-snap-model.md` — game demand model, PFF snaps joined to Catapult load
- `docs/gps-pff-report-pipeline.md` — post-game GPS and PFF report build
- `docs/epa-driven-tendency-method.md` — designed, not built. EPA grades buckets, it does not pick plays.
- `docs/mac-session-handoff.md` — paste-ready prompts for the manual run and both scheduled tasks
- `docs/task-rebinding-2026-09-07.md` — why the tasks failed and what a fix requires

## By week

`docs/weeks/` — one or more docs per opponent.

| Week | Opponent | Docs |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Auburn (L 16-17) | `week1-auburn-result.md`, `week1-auburn-pff-charting.md`, `week1-auburn-qb-accuracy-benchmark.md`, `week1-auburn-fan-reaction.md` |
| 2 | Prairie View A&M | `week2-prairie-view-profile.md` |

## Code and data live elsewhere

This folder holds the project's thinking. The pipelines it describes live in their own
repos:

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `~/DEV/CFB_Victory_Model/` | `matchup/matchup_pull.py`, `coordinators_2026.json`, `frozen_predictions_2026.csv`, 102 cached CFBD CSVs |
| `~/DEV/Football/PFF_Data_Project/` | `keys_grader.py`, PFF ingest, `data/pff.db`, `docs/swagger/` |
| `~/DEV/Catapult_API/` | Catapult reference and the built game reports |
| `~/DEV/DataBase_GPS_Reporting/` | GPS report packages |

Finished weekly deliverables (the .md and .docx a coach sees) go to the OneDrive drive:
`00_Primary_Storage_Drive/01_PROJECTS/_ACTIVE/Weekly_Matchups_2026/Week_N_OPP/`.
See `docs/working-conventions.md`.

## Rules

- Never overwrite an existing file. Append `_v2`, `_v3`.
- Never paste an API key into chat. Read it from the `.env` inside the command.
- PFF and other third-party platforms are read-only. Navigate and read, never edit.
- Writing style: plain and direct, no corporate language, no em dashes, college-freshman
  level explanations, lead with the conclusion. Post-process through the humanizer and
  articulation skills.
- Documents use the Baylor design system: green #154734, gold #FFB81C, Agency FB headers.
- The year is 2026 in this project. Real 2026 dates, 2026 data.

## Working across Claude Code and Cowork

Whatever a future session would need to know goes in `docs/` as a Markdown file and gets
committed. A Cowork session should connect `~/DEV` (or this folder) at the start and write
findings here, not into a cloud project doc. The cloud project is a pointer to this folder,
nothing more.

# STATUS

## Current state
Week 3 (Louisiana Tech at Baylor, Sat Sep 19, 3:00 PM CT) has a preliminary profile at
`docs/weeks/week3-louisiana-tech-profile.md` and nine keys with pass lines at
`docs/weeks/week3-louisiana-tech-keys.md`. Headline: Tech plays man on 31% of dropbacks
and blitzes 52%, the same family as Auburn, so this is the first real test of the Week 1
man-coverage failure. Their front stuffs man blocking (1.21) and gets run over on outside
zone (7.67), which inverts the Week 2 run recommendation.

Week 2 is complete through PFF. `week2-prairie-view-result_v2.md` adds the PFF layer;
`docs/advanced-stats-review-2026-09-13.md` reviews which advanced stats earned their place
after two games. Baylor beat Prairie View A&M 44-3 on Sep 12, 2026. The postgame is
written: `docs/weeks/week2-prairie-view-result.md` (result, keys grading, carry-forward)
and `docs/weeks/week2-prairie-view-capture-filled.md` (the capture sheet backfilled from
play-by-play). All nine keys graded by hand, five hit, three missed, one split.
`~/DEV/CFB_Victory_Model/frozen_predictions_2026.csv` now has both Week 1 (16-17) and
Week 2 (44-3) actuals logged; a dated backup of the pre-edit file sits beside it.
Baylor is 1-1. Week 3 is Louisiana Tech at home, Sep 19. DJ Lagway missed Week 2 with a
one-game injury and is expected back, so the Week 3 offensive brief builds off the Auburn
tape and files the Bennett game as backup-quarterback tape.

## Next
1. Place `2026-09-12_PrairieView-Baylor_Postgame-Review.docx` in the Week 2 folder on the
   primary storage drive. It was built in the Cowork container; the OneDrive path was not
   connected to that session, so it has not been filed yet.
2. Re-run the Week 2 postgame once PFF posts (expected the morning of Sep 13). Baylor-side
   feeds should populate even though PFF does not cover Prairie View. That backfills
   concept-level rushing, coverage-level passing, snap counts and missed tackles, which the
   blank live sheet could not. Write it as a `_v2` doc, do not overwrite.
4. Decide who charts live in Week 3, or drop concept-level rushing and coverage-level
   passing from the weekly package. The Week 2 sheet went in blank and those keys are gone.
5. Refresh `week2-big12-conference-scan.md`. Three games were live and seven unplayed when
   it was captured.
6. Week 3 Keys to Victory are written (`docs/weeks/week3-louisiana-tech-keys.md`, nine keys
   with explicit pass lines). Revisit O1 and O3 once Lagway's status is confirmed, and
   re-check the profile's numbers after BCFToys refreshes.
7. Make a written pre-game call on the frozen line (Baylor +10) versus the market
   (Baylor -17.5). Largest divergence of the season.

## Open questions
- Explosives against man coverage is ungraded for two straight weeks. Either it gets
  charted live or it comes out of the keys framework.
- The Monday scheduled task still does not run. See `task-rebinding-2026-09-07.md`.

## Gotchas
- **`run_direction` is NOT the point of attack.** Use `run_position` (LE/LT/LG/ML/MR/RG/RT/RE)
  for anything about which side of the line. The two disagree on most inside zone carries
  because of cutbacks. This produced a wrong "the right side is broken" finding that reached
  the Week 3 keys before it was caught. Full writeup and corrected numbers in
  `docs/run-direction-vs-point-of-attack.md`.
- **`/v1/video/{league}/games/{id}/plays` is the richest feed on the key**, ~380 fields per
  play, and it is not video. It carries coverage scheme (`pass_coverage_basic` = COVER 0-6),

  script as `./.venv/bin/python matchup/matchup_pull.py`.

- CFBD SP+ returns `ranking: 1` for every team in this pull. Ratings look fine, the rank
  field does not. Do not quote it.
- **PFF DOES cover Prairie View.** The pre-game keys sheet and the v1 result doc both said

  never the assumption. Same class of error as the Week 1 row-zero schema bug.
- Baylor 2026 PFF game ids: wk1 31098 (Auburn), wk2 31122 (PVAMU), wk3 31257 (LA Tech),

- GameOnPaper moved. `gameonpaper.com/cfb/game/{id}` now 301s to `gameonpaper.com/game/{id}`.

- ESPN's `site.api.espn.com/.../summary` endpoint returns Access Denied. Use

- Play-by-play third-down counts run higher than the official box because downs replayed
