metadata.description: Arbitrary metadata to attach to the task

entries.name: TaskUpdate
entries.description:
Use this tool to update a task in the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

**Mark tasks as resolved:**
- When you have completed the work described in a task
- When a task is no longer needed or has been superseded
- IMPORTANT: Always mark your assigned tasks as resolved when you finish them
- After resolving, call TaskList to find your next task

- ONLY mark a task as completed when you have FULLY accomplished it
- If you encounter errors, blockers, or cannot finish, keep the task as in_progress
- When blocked, create a new task describing what needs to be resolved
- Never mark a task as completed if:
  - Tests are failing
  - Implementation is partial
  - You encountered unresolved errors
  - You couldn't find necessary files or dependencies

**Delete tasks:**
- When a task is no longer relevant or was created in error
- Setting status to `deleted` permanently removes the task

**Update task details:**
- When requirements change or become clearer
- When establishing dependencies between tasks

## Fields You Can Update

- **status**: The task status (see Status Workflow below)
- **subject**: Change the task title (imperative form, e.g., "Run tests")
- **description**: Change the task description
- **activeForm**: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")
- **owner**: Change the task owner (agent name)
- **metadata**: Merge metadata keys into the task (set a key to null to delete it)
- **addBlocks**: Mark tasks that cannot start until this one completes
- **addBlockedBy**: Mark tasks that must complete before this one can start

## Status Workflow

Status progresses: `pending` → `in_progress` → `completed`

Use `deleted` to permanently remove a task.

## Staleness

Make sure to read a task's latest state using `TaskGet` before updating it.

## Examples

Mark task as in progress when starting work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "in_progress"}
```

Mark task as completed after finishing work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "completed"}
```

Delete a task:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "deleted"}
```

Claim a task by setting owner:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "owner": "my-name"}
```

Set up task dependencies:
```json
{"taskId": "2", "addBlockedBy": ["1"]}
```

taskId.description: The ID of the task to update

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

addBlocks.description: Task IDs that this task blocks

addBlockedBy.description: Task IDs that block this task

metadata.description: Metadata keys to merge into the task. Set a key to null to delete it.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer
entries.description:
Use a mouse and keyboard to interact with a web browser, and take screenshots. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.
* Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element before moving the cursor.
* If you tried clicking on a program or link but it failed to load, even after waiting, try adjusting your click location so that the tip of the cursor visually falls on the element that you want to click.
* Make sure to click any buttons, links, icons, etc with the cursor tip in the center of the element. Don't click boxes on their edges unless asked.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported and will return an error - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels. Requires a Claude in Chrome extension version that supports scale; older extensions return the full-size image.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tabId.description: Tab ID to execute the action on. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

save_to_disk.description: For screenshot/zoom actions: save the image to disk so it can be attached to a message for the user. Returns the saved path in the tool result. Only set this when you intend to share the image — screenshots you're just looking at don't need saving.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__find
entries.description: Find elements on the page using natural language. Can search for elements by their purpose (e.g., "search bar", "login button") or by text content (e.g., "organic mango product"). Returns up to 20 matching elements with references that can be used with other tools. If more than 20 matches exist, you'll be notified to use a more specific query. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

query.description: Natural language description of what to find (e.g., "search bar", "add to cart button", "product title containing organic")

tabId.description: Tab ID to search in. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__get_page_text
entries.description: Extract raw text content from the page, prioritizing article content. Ideal for reading articles, blog posts, or other text-heavy pages. Returns plain text without HTML formatting. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

tabId.description: Tab ID to extract text from. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__javascript_tool
entries.description: Execute JavaScript code in the context of the current page. The code runs in the page's context and can interact with the DOM, window object, and page variables. Returns the result of the last expression or any thrown errors. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

text.description: The JavaScript code to execute. Evaluated in the page context with REPL semantics: top-level `await` works, and the result of the last expression is returned automatically — write the expression you want (e.g. `window.myData.value`, or `await fetch(url).then(r=>r.json())`) rather than `return ...`. You can access and modify the DOM, call page functions, and interact with page variables.

tabId.description: Tab ID to execute the code in. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate
entries.description: Navigate to a URL, or go forward/back in browser history. tabId may be omitted for URL navigation when calling navigate STANDALONE (not inside browser_batch): tabs_context_mcp{createIfEmpty:true} is called for you and the first tab in the session's group is navigated — its result is appended to this call's output so you have the tab list and ids for subsequent calls. Inside browser_batch, navigate (and other tools that act on a page) requires an explicit tabId. Pass an explicit tabId when you need a specific tab or when the session's group has multiple tabs whose state you must preserve. tabId is required for url:"back"/"forward". A tab opened for you this way is yours to clean up, the same as one from tabs_create_mcp: close it with tabs_close_mcp once you no longer need it and before finishing your task, unless the user asked to see it or wants it kept open.

url.description: The URL to navigate to. Can be provided with or without protocol (defaults to https://). Use "forward" to go forward in history or "back" to go back in history.

tabId.description: Tab ID to navigate. Must be a tab in the current group. If omitted for URL navigation when calling navigate standalone, tabs_context_mcp{createIfEmpty:true} is called for you. Required for url:"back"/"forward" and for navigate (and other tools that act on a page) inside browser_batch.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_network_requests
entries.description: Read HTTP network requests (XHR, Fetch, documents, images, etc.) from a specific tab. Useful for debugging API calls, monitoring network activity, or understanding what requests a page is making. Returns all network requests made by the current page, including cross-origin requests. Requests are automatically cleared when the page navigates to a different domain. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

tabId.description: Tab ID to read network requests from. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

urlPattern.description: Optional URL pattern to filter requests. Only requests whose URL contains this string will be returned (e.g., '/api/' to filter API calls, 'example.com' to filter by domain).

clear.description: If true, clear the network requests after reading to avoid duplicates on subsequent calls. Default is false.

limit.description: Maximum number of requests to return. Defaults to 100. Increase only if you need more results.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page
entries.description: Get an accessibility tree representation of elements on the page. By default returns all elements including non-visible ones. Output is limited to 50000 characters by default. If the output exceeds this limit it is truncated at a line boundary, with a note giving the full size — pass a larger max_chars, or use depth/ref_id to focus on part of the page. Optionally filter for only interactive elements. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

filter.description: Filter elements: "interactive" for buttons/links/inputs only, "all" for all elements including non-visible ones (default: all elements)

tabId.description: Tab ID to read from. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

depth.description: Maximum depth of the tree to traverse (default: 15). Use a smaller depth if output is too large.

ref_id.description: Reference ID of a parent element to read. Will return the specified element and all its children. Use this to focus on a specific part of the page when output is too large.

max_chars.description: Maximum characters for output (default: 50000). Set to a higher value if your client can handle large outputs.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp
entries.description: Close a tab in the MCP tab group by its ID. Use to clean up tabs you're done with. Only tabs in this session's group are closable; call tabs_context_mcp first to get valid IDs. If you close the group's last tab, Chrome auto-removes the group — the next tabs_context_mcp with createIfEmpty starts fresh.

tabId.description: The ID of the tab to close. Must be in this session's tab group. Get valid IDs from tabs_context_mcp.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp
entries.description: Get context information about the current MCP tab group. Returns all tab IDs inside the group if it exists. CRITICAL: You must get the context at least once before using other browser automation tools so you know what tabs exist. Each new conversation should create its own new tab (using tabs_create_mcp) rather than reusing existing tabs, unless the user explicitly asks to use an existing tab.

createIfEmpty.description: Creates a new MCP tab group if none exists, creates a new Window with a new tab group containing an empty tab (which can be used for this conversation). If a MCP tab group already exists, this parameter has no effect.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp
entries.description: Creates a new empty tab in the MCP tab group. CRITICAL: You must get the context using tabs_context_mcp at least once before using other browser automation tools so you know what tabs exist. Tabs you create are yours to clean up: close each one with tabs_close_mcp as soon as you no longer need it, and close any that remain before finishing your task. Leave a tab open only if the user asked to see it or wants it kept open.

# EPA (CFBD PPA) vs EPA (PFF current) vs EPA (PFF legacy) across FBS

Phase 6 put the three sources side by side on Baylor's plays. This asks the harder question: which one predicts later games best?

Every FBS team's EPA per play from its first 6 games predicts the margin of its later games, in 2024, 2025. Plain point margin from the same first games is the baseline: an EPA source earns its keep only if it beats the scoreboard.

- **EPA (CFBD PPA)**: CFBD's Predicted Points Added.
- **EPA (PFF current)**: the number PFF Ultimate displays (PFF release notes, EP/EPA Model Updates, 13 August 2026).
- **EPA (PFF legacy)**: PFF's older GLM model.

## The answer

- **PFF current predicts later margins a little better than CFBD.** r = 0.557 against 0.531, a gap of +0.027 (95% range +0.008 to +0.047). The range stays clear of zero.
- **Plain point margin does about as well.** It reaches r = 0.549; PFF current is +0.008 above it. Over the first games of a season, no EPA source buys much over the scoreboard.
- **2024:** PFF current against CFBD is +0.003 (95% range -0.025 to +0.029); the range crosses zero.
- **2025:** PFF current against CFBD is +0.055 (95% range +0.027 to +0.081); clear of zero.
- **CFBD is the noisiest measure.** Its odd-game against even-game correlation is 0.584, against 0.629 for PFF current and 0.627 for point margin.
- **PFF's 2026 rebuild did not change prediction.** Legacy reaches r = 0.555 against current's 0.557.
- **Removing garbage time does not help.** It lowers r for every source, so the comparison keeps all plays.
- **Winners picked:** CFBD 68.7%, PFF current 69.9%, PFF legacy 70.8%, point margin 69.6% of 674 later games.

For the EPA-driven tendency method, the case for PFF current rests more on data quality than on this edge: it joins Baylor's chart by exact play id and labels lost fumbles correctly (Phase 6).

## Coverage

Games are matched by date and both final scores, never by team name. A tie on a busy Saturday is settled by the teams each PFF code matched in its other games.

| Season | PFF games | CFBD FBS games | Matched | Match rate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2024 | 1,686 | 752 | 751 | 99.9% |
| 2025 | 1,716 | 762 | 762 | 100.0% |

1,509 games are used, after 4 with a source missing a side were dropped. 674 of them are later games for both teams. PFF team codes that matched two different CFBD teams: 0.

The two sources count nearly the same plays: a median of 66 CFBD and 67 PFF scrimmage plays per team-game, with 97.5% within 10% of each other.

r is the correlation between the predictor and the later margin. RMSE is the typical miss in points when a fit from one season predicts the other.

# STATUS

## Current state
Baylor is 1-1. Week 2 (Prairie View A&M 44-3) is written through the PFF layer:
`docs/weeks/week2-prairie-view-result.md`, `_v2.md`, the backfilled capture sheet, and
`docs/weeks/week2-pff-repull-log.md`. Week 3 (Louisiana Tech at Baylor, Sat Sep 19,
3:00 PM CT) has a preliminary profile and nine keys with explicit pass lines in
`docs/weeks/week3-louisiana-tech-*.md`. Both Week 1 and Week 2 actuals are logged in
`~/DEV/CFB_Victory_Model/frozen_predictions_2026.csv`.

A finding was corrected late in the session: `run_direction` is not the point of attack,
and it had produced a wrong "the right side is broken" conclusion that reached Keys O2.
See `docs/run-direction-vs-point-of-attack.md`. The Week 2 v2 doc, the Week 3 profile and
Keys O2 are all corrected and refiled on the storage drive as v2r / v2.

Week 3 headline: Louisiana Tech plays man on 31% of dropbacks and blitzes 52%, the same
family as Auburn, so this is the first real re-test of the Week 1 man-coverage failure.
Their front stops man blocking (1.21) and surrenders outside zone (7.67).

## Next
1. Validate the `missed_tackle_detail` type codes `(M)`, `(B)`, `(O)` against tape. No
   tackling key gets written until those are known rather than inferred.
2. Re-pull PFF game 31122 and write `week2-prairie-view-result_v3.md` if the numbers move.
   The video endpoint already returns 183 plays for that game, so v3 no longer depends on
   `all_blocking` populating.
3. Confirm DJ Lagway's status. Keys O1 and O3 branch on it. He missed Week 2 with a
   one-game injury.
4. Re-pull BCFToys before the Keys are final; on Sep 13 it was still a week stale.
5. Write the pre-game call on the frozen line (Baylor +10) versus the market (-17.5).
6. Act on `docs/advanced-stats-review-2026-09-13.md` for the Week 3 package: replace
   catchable rate with separation-adjusted accuracy, drop the 25% motion target and the
   dependability rating.

## Open questions
- What `(M)`, `(B)`, `(O)` mean in `missed_tackle_detail`. Inference only right now.
- Whether PFF charts `all_blocking` for FBS-vs-FCS games at all. Week 3 is FBS-vs-FBS and
  settles it: if 31257 populates within two days and 31122 still has not, stop promising
  assignment-level analysis for FCS games.
- Two sessions are independently building season-level pulls off the video endpoint, this
  one and whatever is running in `PFF_Data_Project`. Reconcile before either goes further.

## Gotchas
- **`run_direction` is NOT the point of attack.** Use `run_position`
  (LE/LT/LG/ML/MR/RG/RT/RE). They disagree on most inside zone carries because of cutbacks.
- **`/v1/video/{league}/games/{id}/plays`** is the richest feed on the key, ~380 fields per
  play, and it is not video. Coverage scheme (`pass_coverage_basic` = COVER 0-6), tackling
  detail, ST operation timing (`snap_time`, `operation_time`, `fg_optime`, `hang_time`),
  `intended_poa`/`actual_poa`. Only that exact path works; parents 404.
- **PFF DOES cover Prairie View.** Every premium feed for 31122 returns both teams.
- Baylor 2026 PFF game ids: wk1 31098, wk2 31122, wk3 31257, wk4 31278. PFF `gsis_id` is
  not the ESPN id; match on franchise 118 and week.
- **The storage drive is Google Drive, not OneDrive.** `matchup_pull.py` silently created an
  empty duplicate tree under `OneDrive-BaylorUniversity` before it was patched.
- `matchup_pull.py` needs pandas and lxml; run it as
  `~/DEV/CFB_Victory_Model/.venv/bin/python matchup/matchup_pull.py`.
- Getting files from Cowork to the storage drive: `device_commit_files` into
  `~/DEV/_transfer/`, then move with Desktop Commander. Folder-access dialogs have timed out.
- Pushes do not work from the Cowork sandbox shell. Push from the Mac shell.
- CFBD SP+ returns `ranking: 1` for every team. Ratings are fine, the rank field is not.

Baylor Football · Applied Performance · 13 September 2026

Which EPA Source Predicts Best?

We tested 3 sources of EPA on every FBS game of 2024 and 2025. This report tells what we found, in plain words.

The short answer

1

PFF current predicts later games a little better than CFBD. The gain is small but probably real.

2

All of the gain comes from 2025. In 2024, the sources tie.

3

The scoreboard almost ties PFF. Average point margin from the first 6 games predicts almost as well as any EPA source.

4

CFBD data has more errors. For example, CFBD records some lost fumbles as other plays.

5

We recommend EPA (PFF current) for our EPA work. The main reason is cleaner data. The small prediction gain is a second reason.

What is EPA?

EPA means Expected Points Added. It tells how much one play helped or hurt the offense.

Before each play, a computer model gives the offense a number of expected points. This number depends on the down, the yards to go, and the field position. After the play, the model gives a new number. EPA is the new number minus the old number.

Example (numbers for this example only)

Before the play, the offense expects 1.0 point. The quarterback throws a 20-yard catch. Now the offense expects 2.5 points.

EPA for that play is 2.5 − 1.0 = +1.5. A lost fumble gives a large negative EPA.

Different companies build different models. So the same play can get a different EPA from each company. This report asks: which company's EPA is most useful?

The 3 sources we tested

EPA (CFBD PPA)

From CollegeFootballData.com (CFBD), a free public data site. CFBD calls it PPA, Predicted Points Added. It is the same idea as EPA.

EPA (PFF current)

From Pro Football Focus (PFF). This is the number the PFF Ultimate website shows. PFF rebuilt this model on 13 August 2026 (PFF release notes, "EP/EPA Model Updates").

It uses machine learning. Machine learning is a computer method that finds patterns in many past plays.

EPA (PFF legacy)

PFF's older model. It uses a simpler formula. PFF still sends it in the data, so we tested it too.

We always write the source name next to "EPA". An EPA number without its source can mislead.

Test 1: The Baylor check

First, we compared the 3 sources on the same plays. We used Baylor's 25 games from 2024 and 2025. We found 4 things.

  • The sources mostly agree on single plays. The correlation between CFBD and PFF current is 0.88 (see "Words to know" at the end).
  • CFBD gives higher numbers. On average, CFBD is +0.132 points per play above PFF current.
  • CFBD records some lost fumbles wrong. PFF calls 13 plays lost fumbles. CFBD records 7 of them as a different play, such as a catch or a sack. So CFBD scores those 7 plays at +1.16 on average. PFF current scores them at −3.96.
  • PFF connects to our own chart more easily. PFF current connects to 98.6% of our charted plays by exact play ID. CFBD connects to 89.7%, and only by a less exact match.

These differences matter. The source can change which of our play groups look best.

Test 2: The prediction test

A good EPA number should tell us how good a team really is. So a good EPA number should predict the team's later games. We did this test in 6 steps.

  1. We got every play of 2024 and 2025 from PFF (575,497 plays) and from CFBD.
  2. We matched each FBS-against-FBS game in both sources by date and final score. We matched 1,513 of 1,514 games.
  3. We gave each team a rating from its first 6 games. The rating is offense EPA per play minus defense EPA per play allowed.
  4. For each later game, we subtracted one team's rating from the other team's rating. We used that difference to predict the final margin. We used 674 later games.
  5. We did the same test with plain point margin from the first 6 games. This is the scoreboard test. An EPA source is useful only if it beats the scoreboard.
  6. We measured how closely each prediction followed the real margins. For this, we used correlation, written as r.
How to read r

Here, r goes from 0 to 1. A value of 0 means no link. A value of 1 means a perfect link. Football games have much luck, so 0.55 is a good value.

Each result also has a 95% range. We ran the test again 2,000 times on random samples of the games. The range holds the middle 95% of those results. A wide range means we are less sure.

The 4 ranges overlap, so this chart alone cannot pick a winner. A better test compares each source with CFBD on the same random samples. The next chart shows that test.

  • 2024: every range crosses 0. The sources tie.
  • 2025: PFF current, PFF legacy, and the scoreboard all beat CFBD by about 0.05.
  • Both seasons together: PFF current beats CFBD by +0.027 (range +0.008 to +0.047). The scoreboard beats CFBD by +0.018, but its range crosses 0.

In 2025, the scoreboard beat CFBD too. So the 2025 gap may say more about CFBD's data than about PFF's model. PFF's new model and old model gave almost the same results.

Picking winners

Each method picked the winner in about 7 of 10 later games.

MethodWinners pickedGames
EPA (CFBD PPA)68.7%674
EPA (PFF current)69.9%674
EPA (PFF legacy)70.8%674
Point margin (no EPA)69.6%674

The best and the worst differ by about 14 games out of 674. That difference is too small to pick a winner.

Test 3: How steady is each number?

A good rating should not jump around from game to game. To test this, we split each team's season into odd games and even games. Then we compared the 2 halves. A steady number gives similar halves. We used 270 team-seasons with 8 or more games.

MethodOdd games vs even games (r)
EPA (CFBD PPA)0.584
EPA (PFF current)0.629
EPA (PFF legacy)0.629
Point margin (no EPA)0.627

CFBD is the least steady. It is even less steady than the scoreboard. More noise in the data makes a number less steady. This agrees with the fumble errors in Test 1.

Test 4: Does EPA match the same game's score?

We also checked one game at a time. Does a team's EPA in a game follow the margin of that same game? We used 3,018 team-games.

SourceSame-game r
EPA (CFBD PPA)0.892
EPA (PFF current)0.921
EPA (PFF legacy)0.915

Be careful with this result. PFF's release notes say PFF built the new model to match point margin better. So PFF should win this test. This test does not prove that PFF is better. The prediction test (Test 2) is the fairer test.

Garbage time did not help

Garbage time is the part of a game when the winner is already clear. Many analysts remove those plays. We tried this. It made every source a little worse at prediction. So all the results above use all plays.

Limits of this report

  • We have only 2 seasons. 2024 shows a tie. 2025 shows a gain. We need more seasons to know which year is normal.
  • We used the first 6 games only. A longer window can give different results.
  • We did not adjust for opponent strength. A team with easy early games can look too good.
  • The 95% ranges are probably a little too narrow. Games that share a team are not fully separate events.
  • We did not test GameOnPaper. GameOnPaper is a fourth EPA source. It has no data feed that we can pull.
  • Test 1 used 1 team only. We do not know if CFBD's fumble errors are the same for all teams.

What this means for us

Recommendation: use EPA (PFF current)

  • It connects to our own play chart by exact play ID.
  • It records lost fumbles correctly.
  • It predicts later games a little better than CFBD.

Do not say that PFF is "much better". The gain is small. The scoreboard almost ties it. The strongest reason to use PFF is cleaner data, not a better model.

Next steps

  1. Run the prediction test again with 2026 data after the season ends.
  2. Add an adjustment for opponent strength.
  3. Try longer windows than 6 games.

Words to know

EPA
Expected Points Added. The change in expected points from one play.
Expected points
The number of points an offense can expect to score from its down, yards to go, and field position.
Model
A set of computer rules that turns game facts into a number.
FBS
Football Bowl Subdivision. The top level of college football. Baylor plays in the FBS.
Margin
A team's points minus its opponent's points. A 31 to 24 win is a margin of +7.
Correlation (r)
A number that shows how closely 2 sets of numbers move together. Higher means a closer link.
95% range
The span that holds the middle 95% of results when we repeat the test on random samples. It shows how sure we are.
Garbage time
The part of a game when the winner is already clear.
Split-half test
A test that compares a team's odd games with its even games. It shows how steady a number is.

Private. This report uses PFF data. Share it only with Baylor staff.

Data: PFF video plays feed and CFBD play-by-play, 2024 and 2025 regular seasons. Full tables: PlayCalls_SuccessRate_EPA/outputs/EPA_SOURCES_FBS.md and outputs/EPA_SOURCES.md.

Before each play, a computer model gives the offense a number of expected points. This number depends on the down, the yards to go, and the field position. After the play, the model gives a new number. EPA is the new number minus the old number.

Example (numbers for this example only)

Before the play, the offense expects 1.0 point. The quarterback throws a 20-yard catch. Now the offense expects 2.5 points.

EPA for that play is 2.5 − 1.0 = +1.5. A lost fumble gives a large negative EPA.

Different companies build different models. So the same play can get a different EPA from each company. This report asks: which company's EPA is most useful?

The 3 sources we tested

EPA (CFBD PPA)

From CollegeFootballData.com (CFBD), a free public data site. CFBD calls it PPA, Predicted Points Added. It is the same idea as EPA.

EPA (PFF current)

From Pro Football Focus (PFF). This is the number the PFF Ultimate website shows. PFF rebuilt this model on 13 August 2026 (PFF release notes, "EP/EPA Model Updates").

It uses machine learning. Machine learning is a computer method that finds patterns in many past plays.

EPA (PFF legacy)

PFF's older model. It uses a simpler formula. PFF still sends it in the data, so we tested it too.

We always write the source name next to "EPA". An EPA number without its source can mislead.

Test 1: The Baylor check

First, we compared the 3 sources on the same plays. We used Baylor's 25 games from 2024 and 2025. We found 4 things.

  • The sources mostly agree on single plays. The correlation between CFBD and PFF current is 0.88 (see "Words to know" at the end).
  • CFBD gives higher numbers. On average, CFBD is +0.132 points per play above PFF current.
  • CFBD records some lost fumbles wrong. PFF calls 13 plays lost fumbles. CFBD records 7 of them as a different play, such as a catch or a sack. So CFBD scores those 7 plays at +1.16 on average. PFF current scores them at −3.96.
  • PFF connects to our own chart more easily. PFF current connects to 98.6% of our charted plays by exact play ID. CFBD connects to 89.7%, and only by a less exact match.

These differences matter. The source can change which of our play groups look best.

Test 2: The prediction test

A good EPA number should tell us how good a team really is. So a good EPA number should predict the team's later games. We did this test in 6 steps.

  1. We got every play of 2024 and 2025 from PFF (575,497 plays) and from CFBD.
  2. We matched each FBS-against-FBS game in both sources by date and final score. We matched 1,513 of 1,514 games.
  3. We gave each team a rating from its first 6 games. The rating is offense EPA per play minus defense EPA per play allowed.
  4. For each later game, we subtracted one team's rating from the other team's rating. We used that difference to predict the final margin. We used 674 later games.
  5. We did the same test with plain point margin from the first 6 games. This is the scoreboard test. An EPA source is useful only if it beats the scoreboard.
  6. We measured how closely each prediction followed the real margins. For this, we used correlation, written as r.
How to read r

Here, r goes from 0 to 1. A value of 0 means no link. A value of 1 means a perfect link. Football games have much luck, so 0.55 is a good value.

Each result also has a 95% range. We ran the test again 2,000 times on random samples of the games. The range holds the middle 95% of those results. A wide range means we are less sure.

The 4 ranges overlap, so this chart alone cannot pick a winner. A better test compares each source with CFBD on the same random samples. The next chart shows that test.

  • 2024: every range crosses 0. The sources tie.
  • 2025: PFF current, PFF legacy, and the scoreboard all beat CFBD by about 0.05.
  • Both seasons together: PFF current beats CFBD by +0.027 (range +0.008 to +0.047). The scoreboard beats CFBD by +0.018, but its range crosses 0.

In 2025, the scoreboard beat CFBD too. So the 2025 gap may say more about CFBD's data than about PFF's model. PFF's new model and old model gave almost the same results.

Picking winners

Each method picked the winner in about 7 of 10 later games.

MethodWinners pickedGames
EPA (CFBD PPA)68.7%674
EPA (PFF current)69.9%674
EPA (PFF legacy)70.8%674
Point margin (no EPA)69.6%674

The best and the worst differ by about 14 games out of 674. That difference is too small to pick a winner.

Test 3: How steady is each number?

A good rating should not jump around from game to game. To test this, we split each team's season into odd games and even games. Then we compared the 2 halves. A steady number gives similar halves. We used 270 team-seasons with 8 or more games.

MethodOdd games vs even games (r)
EPA (CFBD PPA)0.584
EPA (PFF current)0.629
EPA (PFF legacy)0.629
Point margin (no EPA)0.627

CFBD is the least steady. It is even less steady than the scoreboard. More noise in the data makes a number less steady. This agrees with the fumble errors in Test 1.

Test 4: Does EPA match the same game's score?

We also checked one game at a time. Does a team's EPA in a game follow the margin of that same game? We used 3,018 team-games.

SourceSame-game r
EPA (CFBD PPA)0.892
EPA (PFF current)0.921
EPA (PFF legacy)0.915

Be careful with this result. PFF's release notes say PFF built the new model to match point margin better. So PFF should win this test. This test does not prove that PFF is better. The prediction test (Test 2) is the fairer test.

Garbage time did not help

Garbage time is the part of a game when the winner is already clear. Many analysts remove those plays. We tried this. It made every source a little worse at prediction. So all the results above use all plays.

Limits of this report

  • We have only 2 seasons. 2024 shows a tie. 2025 shows a gain. We need more seasons to know which year is normal.
  • We used the first 6 games only. A longer window can give different results.
  • We did not adjust for opponent strength. A team with easy early games can look too good.
  • The 95% ranges are probably a little too narrow. Games that share a team are not fully separate events.
  • We did not test GameOnPaper. GameOnPaper is a fourth EPA source. It has no data feed that we can pull.
  • Test 1 used 1 team only. We do not know if CFBD's fumble errors are the same for all teams.

What this means for us

Recommendation: use EPA (PFF current)

  • It connects to our own play chart by exact play ID.
  • It records lost fumbles correctly.
  • It predicts later games a little better than CFBD.

Do not say that PFF is "much better". The gain is small. The scoreboard almost ties it. The strongest reason to use PFF is cleaner data, not a better model.

Next steps

  1. Run the prediction test again with 2026 data after the season ends.
  2. Add an adjustment for opponent strength.
  3. Try longer windows than 6 games.

Words to know

EPA
Expected Points Added. The change in expected points from one play.
Expected points
The number of points an offense can expect to score from its down, yards to go, and field position.
Model
A set of computer rules that turns game facts into a number.
FBS
Football Bowl Subdivision. The top level of college football. Baylor plays in the FBS.
Margin
A team's points minus its opponent's points. A 31 to 24 win is a margin of +7.
Correlation (r)
A number that shows how closely 2 sets of numbers move together. Higher means a closer link.
95% range
The span that holds the middle 95% of results when we repeat the test on random samples. It shows how sure we are.
Garbage time
The part of a game when the winner is already clear.
Split-half test
A test that compares a team's odd games with its even games. It shows how steady a number is.

Private. This report uses PFF data. Share it only with Baylor staff.

Data: PFF video plays feed and CFBD play-by-play, 2024 and 2025 regular seasons. Full tables: PlayCalls_SuccessRate_EPA/outputs/EPA_SOURCES_FBS.md and outputs/EPA_SOURCES.md.

1	# EPA-driven tendency analysis (PFF join) — design note
2	
3	Status: designed, not built. No data has been pulled. Origin: Eric's idea, discussed 2026-09-06.
4	
5	## The original idea
6	Use CFBD play-by-play and GameOnPaper EPA to find plays where a team had very high EPA,
7	or where high-EPA plays clustered. Look those specific plays up in PFF, read the formation,
8	and build tendencies from there. EPA decides which plays are worth studying.
9	
10	## The core insight worth keeping
11	Frequency tells you what a team does. EPA tells you what actually hurts. Nearly every
12	tendency report a coach receives is frequency-based and ranks nothing by consequence.
13	Weighting tendencies by EPA is the part of this idea with real value.
14	
15	## Why the original mechanism was changed
16	Single-play EPA is mostly noise. A 45-yard gain may be scheme or may be a missed tackle.
17	Sorting a season by EPA and pulling the top N plays selects on outcome, which means
18	scheming against variance. It also leaves roughly 20 plays spread across a dozen
19	formations, which is not enough to call anything a tendency.
20	
21	Clustered EPA is less noisy than single spikes, but drive-level clusters often reflect
22	script, tempo, or field position rather than a scheme the offense is good at.
23	
24	## The method instead: EPA grades buckets, it does not pick plays
25	1. Define buckets from PFF charting: personnel, formation, backfield alignment,
26	   motion yes/no, down and distance band, field zone.
27	2. Attach EPA to every play, not only the exciting ones.
28	3. Per bucket, compute frequency, EPA per play, success rate, and sample size.
29	4. Shrink each bucket's EPA toward the team mean based on sample size (empirical Bayes,
30	   or a simple sample-weighted blend). A 6-play bucket at +0.8 gets pulled hard toward
31	   the mean. A 70-play bucket at +0.35 barely moves.
32	5. Rank by leverage: shrunk EPA multiplied by frequency. That surfaces what a team does
33	   often AND does well, which is what you game-plan against.
34	
35	Target output reads like: "On 2nd and medium from 12 personnel with a tight end wing,
36	they are +0.31 EPA per play on 58 snaps, and it is 19% of their 2nd down calls."
37	
38	## Known risks
39	**The join is the hard part.** PFF and CFBD/ESPN share no play ID. Match on game, quarter,
40	clock, down, distance, and yard line with a fuzzy time window. Expect 90 to 95% clean,
41	then hand-resolve penalties, no-plays, and clock discrepancies. Budget roughly a week
42	before a single insight appears. Report the match rate before looking at any result; a
43	biased join silently drops penalties and no-plays, and those cluster.
44	
45	**Use one EPA model.** CFBD EPA and GameOnPaper's ESPN-based EPA are different models and
46	return different values for the same play. Decision: CFBD EPA is the single input.
47	GameOnPaper becomes a cross-check, not a second source.
48	
49	**Sample size at one game.** About 65 to 75 offensive snaps, leaving 4 to 8 plays per
50	bucket. Enough to prove the pipeline works, not enough to call a tendency. If the join
51	holds, the next step is the opponent's full season, roughly 800 snaps.
52	
53	**Licensing.** PFF-derived data stays internal to the department.
54	
55	## Adoption risk
56	Football analytics products die from workflow fit, not bad math. A tool requiring a coach
57	to change how he preps on Tuesday loses to a worse tool that fits the existing sheet.
58	The football staff already has PFF and analysts. If this is built for them, the bar is
59	beating what the QCs already produce on Sunday night.
60	
61	An alternative lane worth considering: layer EPA-weighted situational context onto GPS and
62	workload data (which situations produce the highest-cost snaps, how scheme tendencies map
63	to practice load and exposure). Eric owns both the customer and the data there.
64	
65	## Pilot: Baylor vs Houston, November 2025
66	Chosen because Houston is a conference opponent likely to recur, so the join code and
67	bucket logic get reused rather than thrown away. Treat the run as a plumbing test, not an
68	answer about Houston.
69	
70	Steps: get ESPN and CFBD game IDs (check the 102 cached CSVs in CFB_Victory_Model first)
71	→ pull play-by-play with EPA → load the PFF export → build and validate the join, report
72	match rate → bucket, shrink, rank → review top rows.
73	
74	## Blockers as of 2026-09-06
75	1. **PFF export.** Unresolved and it gates everything. Needs a play-level CSV for the game
76	   with formation and personnel. Without it this becomes an EPA-only situational study,
77	   which does not test the idea.
78	2. **Folder access.** The macOS folder dialog timed out twice, so `~/DEV` and
79	   `Weekly_Matchups_2026` were never reachable. Nothing ran on the Mac.
80	3. **Audience.** Football staff, or Eric's to own? Decides whether the join work is worth
81	   doing at all.
82	
83	## Environment note
84	The cloud container is IP-blocked by ESPN (403 from ESPN's edge, not a user-agent problem).
85	All ESPN and GameOnPaper work must run on the Mac through the local shell.

# EPA-driven tendency analysis (PFF join) — design note

Status: designed, not built. No data has been pulled. Origin: Eric's idea, discussed 2026-09-06.

## The original idea
Use CFBD play-by-play and GameOnPaper EPA to find plays where a team had very high EPA,
or where high-EPA plays clustered. Look those specific plays up in PFF, read the formation,
and build tendencies from there. EPA decides which plays are worth studying.

## The core insight worth keeping
Frequency tells you what a team does. EPA tells you what actually hurts. Nearly every
tendency report a coach receives is frequency-based and ranks nothing by consequence.
Weighting tendencies by EPA is the part of this idea with real value.

## Why the original mechanism was changed
Single-play EPA is mostly noise. A 45-yard gain may be scheme or may be a missed tackle.
Sorting a season by EPA and pulling the top N plays selects on outcome, which means
scheming against variance. It also leaves roughly 20 plays spread across a dozen
formations, which is not enough to call anything a tendency.

Clustered EPA is less noisy than single spikes, but drive-level clusters often reflect
script, tempo, or field position rather than a scheme the offense is good at.

## The method instead: EPA grades buckets, it does not pick plays
1. Define buckets from PFF charting: personnel, formation, backfield alignment,
   motion yes/no, down and distance band, field zone.
2. Attach EPA to every play, not only the exciting ones.
3. Per bucket, compute frequency, EPA per play, success rate, and sample size.
4. Shrink each bucket's EPA toward the team mean based on sample size (empirical Bayes,
   or a simple sample-weighted blend). A 6-play bucket at +0.8 gets pulled hard toward
   the mean. A 70-play bucket at +0.35 barely moves.
5. Rank by leverage: shrunk EPA multiplied by frequency. That surfaces what a team does
   often AND does well, which is what you game-plan against.

Target output reads like: "On 2nd and medium from 12 personnel with a tight end wing,
they are +0.31 EPA per play on 58 snaps, and it is 19% of their 2nd down calls."

## Known risks
**The join is the hard part.** PFF and CFBD/ESPN share no play ID. Match on game, quarter,
clock, down, distance, and yard line with a fuzzy time window. Expect 90 to 95% clean,
then hand-resolve penalties, no-plays, and clock discrepancies. Budget roughly a week
before a single insight appears. Report the match rate before looking at any result; a
biased join silently drops penalties and no-plays, and those cluster.

**Use one EPA model.** CFBD EPA and GameOnPaper's ESPN-based EPA are different models and
return different values for the same play. Decision: CFBD EPA is the single input.
GameOnPaper becomes a cross-check, not a second source.

**Sample size at one game.** About 65 to 75 offensive snaps, leaving 4 to 8 plays per
bucket. Enough to prove the pipeline works, not enough to call a tendency. If the join
holds, the next step is the opponent's full season, roughly 800 snaps.

**Licensing.** PFF-derived data stays internal to the department.

## Adoption risk
Football analytics products die from workflow fit, not bad math. A tool requiring a coach
to change how he preps on Tuesday loses to a worse tool that fits the existing sheet.
The football staff already has PFF and analysts. If this is built for them, the bar is
beating what the QCs already produce on Sunday night.

An alternative lane worth considering: layer EPA-weighted situational context onto GPS and
workload data (which situations produce the highest-cost snaps, how scheme tendencies map
to practice load and exposure). Eric owns both the customer and the data there.

# EPA-driven tendency analysis (PFF join) — design note

Status: designed, not built. No data has been pulled. Origin: Eric's idea, discussed 2026-09-06.

## The original idea
Use CFBD play-by-play and GameOnPaper EPA to find plays where a team had very high EPA,
or where high-EPA plays clustered. Look those specific plays up in PFF, read the formation,
and build tendencies from there. EPA decides which plays are worth studying.

## The core insight worth keeping
Frequency tells you what a team does. EPA tells you what actually hurts. Nearly every
tendency report a coach receives is frequency-based and ranks nothing by consequence.
Weighting tendencies by EPA is the part of this idea with real value.

## Why the original mechanism was changed
Single-play EPA is mostly noise. A 45-yard gain may be scheme or may be a missed tackle.
Sorting a season by EPA and pulling the top N plays selects on outcome, which means
scheming against variance. It also leaves roughly 20 plays spread across a dozen
formations, which is not enough to call anything a tendency.

Clustered EPA is less noisy than single spikes, but drive-level clusters often reflect
script, tempo, or field position rather than a scheme the offense is good at.

## The method instead: EPA grades buckets, it does not pick plays
1. Define buckets from PFF charting: personnel, formation, backfield alignment,
   motion yes/no, down and distance band, field zone.
2. Attach EPA to every play, not only the exciting ones.
3. Per bucket, compute frequency, EPA per play, success rate, and sample size.
4. Shrink each bucket's EPA toward the team mean based on sample size (empirical Bayes,
   or a simple sample-weighted blend). A 6-play bucket at +0.8 gets pulled hard toward
   the mean. A 70-play bucket at +0.35 barely moves.
5. Rank by leverage: shrunk EPA multiplied by frequency. That surfaces what a team does
   often AND does well, which is what you game-plan against.

Target output reads like: "On 2nd and medium from 12 personnel with a tight end wing,
they are +0.31 EPA per play on 58 snaps, and it is 19% of their 2nd down calls."

## Known risks
**The join is the hard part.** PFF and CFBD/ESPN share no play ID. Match on game, quarter,
clock, down, distance, and yard line with a fuzzy time window. Expect 90 to 95% clean,
then hand-resolve penalties, no-plays, and clock discrepancies. Budget roughly a week
before a single insight appears. Report the match rate before looking at any result; a
biased join silently drops penalties and no-plays, and those cluster.

**Use one EPA model.** CFBD EPA and GameOnPaper's ESPN-based EPA are different models and
return different values for the same play. Decision: CFBD EPA is the single input.
GameOnPaper becomes a cross-check, not a second source.

**Sample size at one game.** About 65 to 75 offensive snaps, leaving 4 to 8 plays per
bucket. Enough to prove the pipeline works, not enough to call a tendency. If the join
holds, the next step is the opponent's full season, roughly 800 snaps.

**Licensing.** PFF-derived data stays internal to the department.

## Adoption risk
Football analytics products die from workflow fit, not bad math. A tool requiring a coach
to change how he preps on Tuesday loses to a worse tool that fits the existing sheet.
The football staff already has PFF and analysts. If this is built for them, the bar is
beating what the QCs already produce on Sunday night.

An alternative lane worth considering: layer EPA-weighted situational context onto GPS and
workload data (which situations produce the highest-cost snaps, how scheme tendencies map
to practice load and exposure). Eric owns both the customer and the data there.

## Pilot: Baylor vs Houston, November 2025
Chosen because Houston is a conference opponent likely to recur, so the join code and
bucket logic get reused rather than thrown away. Treat the run as a plumbing test, not an
answer about Houston.

Steps: get ESPN and CFBD game IDs (check the 102 cached CSVs in CFB_Victory_Model first)
→ pull play-by-play with EPA → load the PFF export → build and validate the join, report
match rate → bucket, shrink, rank → review top rows.

## Blockers as of 2026-09-06
1. **PFF export.** Unresolved and it gates everything. Needs a play-level CSV for the game
   with formation and personnel. Without it this becomes an EPA-only situational study,
   which does not test the idea.
2. **Folder access.** The macOS folder dialog timed out twice, so `~/DEV` and
   `Weekly_Matchups_2026` were never reachable. Nothing ran on the Mac.
3. **Audience.** Football staff, or Eric's to own? Decides whether the join work is worth
   doing at all.

## Environment note
The cloud container is IP-blocked by ESPN (403 from ESPN's edge, not a user-agent problem).
All ESPN and GameOnPaper work must run on the Mac through the local shell.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/closeout

# Closeout

One command that replaces the manual end-of-day sequence: "any loose ends?" → "commit and push what needs to be" → "is this in memory?" → "write a handoff so Codex can pick this up."

Run all five checks, then give ONE verdict. Do not ask permission between steps — the invocation of this skill IS the authorization for the full sequence. Commit and push is standing-authorized for every DEV repo: each repo's `AGENTS.md` Session routine says "update STATUS, commit, push at end", and unpushed work on one machine is the top cause of conflicts on the other. The only exceptions are repos whose `CLAUDE.md` says their data must stay local (DexaProject is the precedent); commit those locally and list them as open.

## Step 1 — Loose-ends sweep

- `git status` in every repo touched this session (check cwd first, then any repo mentioned in the conversation; if session context is thin, check `KeystoneOS` and any `DEV/` repo with commits dated today).
- Unfinished todos/tasks from this session (TaskList if available).
- Background jobs or workflows still running.
- Anything the user was promised earlier in the session that wasn't delivered.

## Step 2 — Commit & push

- Every repo touched this session: stage, commit with a descriptive message, `git pull --no-rebase` (the other machine may have pushed), push. If the merge conflicts, keep this machine's version and save the remote copy beside it as `<file>.from-mac` / `<file>.from-windows`, then push and list the file under "Still open".
- Before staging, make sure any new file over 95 MB and any `.env` is in `.gitignore`.
- Local-only repos (CLAUDE.md says so): commit, do not push, list it.
- Also check the three config repos, `~/.claude` (dotclaude), `~/.claude/skills` (claude-skills) and `~/.claude/global-memory` (claude-global-memory). If any has changes, commit and push it the same way, so the other machine's `/dev-sync` picks it up.
- **Push `global-memory` even on a light session.** `daily-backup` pushes it nightly, which is too late for a same-day handoff: work the Mac in the afternoon, sit down at Windows that evening, and anything written to MEMORY.md or handoffs is still only on the Mac. Pushing it here is what makes memory available to the other machine tonight rather than tomorrow. It is the only repo that carries memory across, so treat an unpushed `global-memory` the same as an unpushed project repo: it blocks "clear to sign off".
- Nothing to commit → say so in one line, move on.

## Step 3 — Memory verification

- Check `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log` — must be empty. If not, surface contents and fix the hook issue if obvious.
- Confirm today's transcript file exists at `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/<today>.md` and was modified within the last few hours.
- Run the dev-docs harvest so repo docs reach memsearch: `bash ~/.claude/scripts/harvest-dev-docs.sh` (Mac) or `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $HOME\.claude\scripts\harvest-dev-docs.ps1` (Windows). It copies every repo's `docs/*.md` into `~/.claude/global-memory/dev-docs/`, which is on the index list. One line of output; do this after Step 4 so today's STATUS is included.
- If this session produced a durable decision or new active thread, update `~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (respect the 2,500-char cap; consolidate before adding) or write a Tier A memory file per the memory-system rules in CLAUDE.md.
- **Tier A does not cross machines — mirror it or lose it.** Project memory lives under a slug built from the project's absolute path, and that path differs on the Mac and the Windows laptop, so a Tier A file written today is not auto-injected tomorrow on the other machine. Global memory and the repo both cross; Tier A does not. So for every Tier A fact written this session, ask: is this durable and project-scoped? If yes, it must also land in the repo — `docs/STATUS.md` for current state, `docs/DECISIONS.md` for a decision and its reasoning, the dated handoff for the detail. Treat Tier A as a fast local cache and the repo as the record. If a fact only ever exists in Tier A, assume the other machine will never see it.

## Step 4 — Cross-harness handoff

This is the **canonical durable handoff** — the one future sessions and other harnesses read. (For a mid-session, chat-only summary before `/clear`, that's the `session-handoff` skill; the mattpocock `handoff` skill writes to the OS temp dir and is not durable — don't rely on it for cross-session state.)

If real work happened this session (not just Q&A), write a handoff to
`<repo>/docs/handoffs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md` (or `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/` if no repo fits):

- What was being worked on and why
- Decisions made (with the reasoning that would be lost)
- Exact file paths of everything created or modified this session
- Next actions, most important first
- Anything mid-flight (open questions, awaited inputs)

Plain markdown, no harness-specific syntax — Codex, Antigravity, or a fresh Claude session must be able to resume from it. Commit it with the Step 2 commit when in a repo.

**Always, in every repo touched (even for light sessions): update `docs/STATUS.md`.** It is the file the next session reads first, on either machine, in any harness. Rewrite the sections in place, keep it short:

- `## Current state` — two to five lines on where things stand today
- `## Next` — most important first
- `## Open questions` — decisions waiting on Eric
- `## Gotchas` — anything that will bite the next session

The dated handoff file is the detailed record; STATUS.md is the summary. Do Step 4 before the Step 2 commit so both land in the same push.

## Step 5 — Verdict

End with a single short report:

```
## Closeout — <date>

**Committed & pushed:** <repos + one-line summary, or "nothing to commit">
**STATUS.md:** updated in <repos>
**Memory:** captured ✓ / issue found: <what>
**Handoff:** <path, or "not needed — no substantive work">
**Still open:** <numbered list, or "none">

Clear to sign off. / Not clear: <the one thing blocking>.
```

"Clear to sign off" means: every touched repo is pushed (or is a declared local-only repo). If anything is unpushed, the verdict is "Not clear" and the unpushed repo is the one thing blocking.

Every file created or modified during the session must appear somewhere in the report with its full path — "where did this save?" should never need to be asked.

## Rules

- Push every touched DEV repo. Do not leave the laptop with unpushed work; the other machine pulls from GitHub, not from this disk.
- Never skip Step 3 — memory capture failing silently is the user's top recurring worry.
- If a check fails and the fix is quick and safe (restage a file, clear a stale lock), fix it and note it. If the fix is risky, list it under "Still open" instead.
- Total output should fit on one screen. The user is leaving; brevity is the deliverable.

  margin reaches 0.549. CFBD is the least steady measure.

3. Try windows longer than 6 games.

- None waiting on Eric.

- PFF `off_score`/`def_score` are the score BEFORE the snap; CFBD's are after the play.
- Common final scores repeat on a Saturday. `fbs.match_games` needs its second pass (team
  codes learned from unique matches) or the match rate drops to about 68%.
- Removing garbage time lowers r for every source. Do not switch to the clean variant.
- Bootstrap ranges run a little narrow: games that share a team are not independent.
- This repo holds no PFF credentials. It reads PFF_Data_Project's parquet read-only.

# Handoff 2026-09-13: which EPA source, and the decision to use PFF

Claude Code session on the Mac (background job). Ran alongside the Cowork session that did
Week 2 and Week 3 (`2026-09-13-week2-pff-week3-latech-and-a-correction.md`).

## What was worked on and why
Eric asked whether the matchup work used PFF or CFBD EPA, then asked for a test of which
EPA source is best. The work ran in three repos:

1. **PFF_Data_Project**: found PFF EPA in the Video Feeds plays endpoint
   (`expected_points_added` = PFF current, `expected_points_added_legacy` = PFF legacy),
   ingested Baylor 2024-2025, then streamed the full 2024 and 2025 FBS seasons to parquet.
2. **PlayCalls_SuccessRate_EPA Phase 6**: Baylor 2024-2025, play-level comparison of
   CFBD PPA, PFF current and PFF legacy.
3. **PlayCalls_SuccessRate_EPA Phase 7**: every 2024-2025 FBS-vs-FBS game. Each team's first
   6 games predict later margins; plain point margin is the baseline.

## Findings
- PFF release notes ("EP/EPA Model Updates", 2026-08-13): current is the XGBoost rebuild
  that PFF Ultimate displays; legacy is the older GLM.
- Baylor: CFBD sits +0.132 per play above PFF current. CFBD records 7 of PFF's 13 lost
  fumbles as other plays. PFF attaches to 98.6% of charted plays by exact play id; CFBD
  reaches 89.7% by fuzzy match.
- FBS: PFF current r 0.557 vs CFBD 0.531 (gap +0.027, 95% +0.008 to +0.047). 2024 is a
  tie; 2025 carries the whole gap. Point margin alone reaches 0.549. Split-half: CFBD 0.584,
  PFF 0.629, points 0.627. Legacy tracks current. Removing garbage time hurts every source.
- Same-game fit favors PFF (0.921 vs 0.892), but PFF tuned the model to point differential,
  so that is not independent evidence.

## Decisions
- **EPA (PFF current) is the single EPA source (Eric, 2026-09-13).** Replaces the 9/06
  "CFBD EPA is the single input" line. Main reason is data quality (exact play-id join,
  correct fumbles), the small prediction edge second. CFBD PPA and GameOnPaper are labeled
  cross-checks; GameOnPaper remains the only option for live in-game EPA.
- Do not describe PFF as "much better": the scoreboard nearly ties it.

  (Eric chose this over leaving only the correction note).

This is the whole fix. Both tasks are registered and say `Ready`, but they have
**no trigger**, so they will never fire on their own.

Do **not** use `schtasks /Change` — it cannot add a schedule type to an existing
task. Use the PowerShell module.

Two triggers each, on purpose:

- `-AtLogOn` — catches you whenever you sit down
- a time trigger — the regular cadence
- `-StartWhenAvailable` — a slot missed because the laptop was asleep runs on wake

```powershell
# Weekly DEV backup — Sundays 18:00, plus at logon
$devTriggers = @(
  (New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -Weekly -DaysOfWeek Sunday -At 6pm),
  (New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -AtLogOn -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME")
)
Set-ScheduledTask -TaskName "Backup DEV to Drive" `
  -Trigger $devTriggers `
  -Settings (New-ScheduledTaskSettingsSet -StartWhenAvailable -ExecutionTimeLimit (New-TimeSpan -Hours 4))

# Daily AI session backup — 17:30, plus at logon
$aiTriggers = @(
  (New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -Daily -At 5:30pm),
  (New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -AtLogOn -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME")
)
Set-ScheduledTask -TaskName "Backup AI Sessions to Drive" `
  -Trigger $aiTriggers `

```

Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/closeout

# Closeout

One command that replaces the manual end-of-day sequence: "any loose ends?" → "commit and push what needs to be" → "is this in memory?" → "write a handoff so Codex can pick this up."

Run all five checks, then give ONE verdict. Do not ask permission between steps — the invocation of this skill IS the authorization for the full sequence. Commit and push is standing-authorized for every DEV repo: each repo's `AGENTS.md` Session routine says "update STATUS, commit, push at end", and unpushed work on one machine is the top cause of conflicts on the other. The only exceptions are repos whose `CLAUDE.md` says their data must stay local (DexaProject is the precedent); commit those locally and list them as open.

## Step 1 — Loose-ends sweep

- `git status` in every repo touched this session (check cwd first, then any repo mentioned in the conversation; if session context is thin, check `KeystoneOS` and any `DEV/` repo with commits dated today).
- Unfinished todos/tasks from this session (TaskList if available).
- Background jobs or workflows still running.
- Anything the user was promised earlier in the session that wasn't delivered.

## Step 2 — Commit & push

- Every repo touched this session: stage, commit with a descriptive message, `git pull --no-rebase` (the other machine may have pushed), push. If the merge conflicts, keep this machine's version and save the remote copy beside it as `<file>.from-mac` / `<file>.from-windows`, then push and list the file under "Still open".
- Before staging, make sure any new file over 95 MB and any `.env` is in `.gitignore`.
- Local-only repos (CLAUDE.md says so): commit, do not push, list it.
- Also check the three config repos, `~/.claude` (dotclaude), `~/.claude/skills` (claude-skills) and `~/.claude/global-memory` (claude-global-memory). If any has changes, commit and push it the same way, so the other machine's `/dev-sync` picks it up.
- **Push `global-memory` even on a light session.** `daily-backup` pushes it nightly, which is too late for a same-day handoff: work the Mac in the afternoon, sit down at Windows that evening, and anything written to MEMORY.md or handoffs is still only on the Mac. Pushing it here is what makes memory available to the other machine tonight rather than tomorrow. It is the only repo that carries memory across, so treat an unpushed `global-memory` the same as an unpushed project repo: it blocks "clear to sign off".
- Nothing to commit → say so in one line, move on.

## Step 3 — Memory verification

- Check `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log` — must be empty. If not, surface contents and fix the hook issue if obvious.
- Confirm today's transcript file exists at `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/<today>.md` and was modified within the last few hours.
- Run the dev-docs harvest so repo docs reach memsearch: `bash ~/.claude/scripts/harvest-dev-docs.sh` (Mac) or `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $HOME\.claude\scripts\harvest-dev-docs.ps1` (Windows). It copies every repo's `docs/*.md` into `~/.claude/global-memory/dev-docs/`, which is on the index list. One line of output; do this after Step 4 so today's STATUS is included.
- If this session produced a durable decision or new active thread, update `~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (respect the 2,500-char cap; consolidate before adding) or write a Tier A memory file per the memory-system rules in CLAUDE.md.
- **Tier A does not cross machines — mirror it or lose it.** Project memory lives under a slug built from the project's absolute path, and that path differs on the Mac and the Windows laptop, so a Tier A file written today is not auto-injected tomorrow on the other machine. Global memory and the repo both cross; Tier A does not. So for every Tier A fact written this session, ask: is this durable and project-scoped? If yes, it must also land in the repo — `docs/STATUS.md` for current state, `docs/DECISIONS.md` for a decision and its reasoning, the dated handoff for the detail. Treat Tier A as a fast local cache and the repo as the record. If a fact only ever exists in Tier A, assume the other machine will never see it.

## Step 4 — Cross-harness handoff

This is the **canonical durable handoff** — the one future sessions and other harnesses read. (For a mid-session, chat-only summary before `/clear`, that's the `session-handoff` skill; the mattpocock `handoff` skill writes to the OS temp dir and is not durable — don't rely on it for cross-session state.)

If real work happened this session (not just Q&A), write a handoff to
`<repo>/docs/handoffs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md` (or `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/` if no repo fits):

- What was being worked on and why
- Decisions made (with the reasoning that would be lost)
- Exact file paths of everything created or modified this session
- Next actions, most important first
- Anything mid-flight (open questions, awaited inputs)

Plain markdown, no harness-specific syntax — Codex, Antigravity, or a fresh Claude session must be able to resume from it. Commit it with the Step 2 commit when in a repo.

**Always, in every repo touched (even for light sessions): update `docs/STATUS.md`.** It is the file the next session reads first, on either machine, in any harness. Rewrite the sections in place, keep it short:

- `## Current state` — two to five lines on where things stand today
- `## Next` — most important first
- `## Open questions` — decisions waiting on Eric
- `## Gotchas` — anything that will bite the next session

The dated handoff file is the detailed record; STATUS.md is the summary. Do Step 4 before the Step 2 commit so both land in the same push.

## Step 5 — Verdict

End with a single short report:

```
## Closeout — <date>

**Committed & pushed:** <repos + one-line summary, or "nothing to commit">
**STATUS.md:** updated in <repos>
**Memory:** captured ✓ / issue found: <what>
**Handoff:** <path, or "not needed — no substantive work">
**Still open:** <numbered list, or "none">

Clear to sign off. / Not clear: <the one thing blocking>.
```

"Clear to sign off" means: every touched repo is pushed (or is a declared local-only repo). If anything is unpushed, the verdict is "Not clear" and the unpushed repo is the one thing blocking.

Every file created or modified during the session must appear somewhere in the report with its full path — "where did this save?" should never need to be asked.

## Rules

- Push every touched DEV repo. Do not leave the laptop with unpushed work; the other machine pulls from GitHub, not from this disk.
- Never skip Step 3 — memory capture failing silently is the user's top recurring worry.
- If a check fails and the fix is quick and safe (restage a file, clear a stale lock), fix it and note it. If the fix is risky, list it under "Still open" instead.
- Total output should fit on one screen. The user is leaving; brevity is the deliverable.

# Handoff 2026-09-13: refresh_all_data.bat and its Windows task

Claude Code session on the Mac, guiding Eric through commands on the Windows laptop.

## What was worked on and why
Windows reported that the `.bat` file for the `Refresh_All_Data` scheduled task does not
exist. `refresh_all_data.bat` lives in `_INBOX`, not the DEV root, and the old task still
points at the old path. Eric's first guess (dev-sync pulled before the Mac pushed) was
ruled out: commit `f7246b0` was on GitHub before the sync, and dev-sync never deletes.

## Decisions and reasoning
- **Replace the `wmic` date line with PowerShell `Get-Date -Format yyyy-MM-dd`.** `wmic` is
  removed from newer Windows 11, which likely killed the ForcePlate and Perch steps since
  2026-04-30. The bat now stops with an error if no date comes back. Tested the PowerShell
  command on the Mac (prints `2026-09-13`); the bat itself has not run on Windows since.
- **Do not change the old task; register a new one.** `schtasks /change` on
  `Refresh_All_Data` gave "Access is denied" even with the password. The laptop has no admin
  rights, and the old task was likely set to run whether logged on or not. A task
  registered with `Register-ScheduledTask` without `-User` runs as Eric, interactive, and
  needs no admin and no password. Same pattern as the backup tasks.
- New task: `\Eric\Refresh All Data`, daily, `-StartWhenAvailable`, 2-hour limit, working
  directory `_INBOX`. Registered at 6:00 AM (Claude's pick) and shown Ready.

# Machine

Machine-specific shell, paths, and traps live in `~/.claude/machine.md` (gitignored; copy `machine.macos.md` or `machine.windows.md` to `machine.md` on a new machine). It is imported below.

@machine.md

Two machines share this setup: the MacBook (`~/DEV`) and the Baylor Windows laptop (`~/Desktop/DEV`). Projects sync through GitHub (`erash11`), documents through Google Drive. Every project repo carries a Session routine in its `AGENTS.md`: `git pull` + read `docs/STATUS.md` at start; update `STATUS.md`, commit, `git push` at end.
# Workflow Expectations

- When asked to **create, merge, or consolidate an artifact** (calendar, deck, doc), the expected deliverable is always a produced file. Verify what exists first, then create the artifact regardless — never conclude with "it already exists" instead of delivering the file.
- When the user types `/graphify`, invoke the Skill tool with `skill: "graphify"` before doing anything else.

# Session Startup

Handled by the `keystone-unified-snapshot.js` SessionStart hook — do not read these files by hand. It injects `global-memory/USER.md`, `global-memory/MEMORY.md`, `transcripts/.errors.log` (only when non-empty), and a pointer to the KeystoneOS snapshot.

- If `.errors.log` content appears, surface it once on the first response, then continue. It is normally empty; entries mean hook failures.
- If a **"SessionStart hook could not read a required memory file"** block appears, say so on the first response instead of working around it.
- **If no `## User profile` block is in context at session start, the hook did not fire.** Say so, then read `USER.md`, `MEMORY.md` and `transcripts/.errors.log` by hand.
- What the hook injects is a frozen snapshot. Mid-session writes take effect next session. Never load more than this proactively.

# Memory — routing only

The two-tier memory system (`~/.claude/global-memory/` and `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`) is owned by the **`memory-write` skill**, which holds the tier rules, character caps, slug rules, write steps, retrieval ladder, and daily-compiled-log rules.

The active project's Tier A memory (`~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`, indexed by its `MEMORY.md`) is **auto-injected by the harness** each session. Tier A files are also indexed by memsearch, so they stay recallable across projects.

- Writing a fact — "remember this", "note that", "save this", "forget about" → `Skill("memory-write")`
- Recalling past context — "did we already…?", "what did we decide about X" → `Skill("memory-write")`, retrieval-ladder section
- Daily compiled logs at `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/daily/` are owned by `claude-memory-compiler`. Never hand-edit them; never read them eagerly.
- **Slugs differ per machine** (Mac `-Users-kristinarash-DEV-<X>`, Windows `C--Users-eric-rash-Desktop-DEV-<X>`). Tier A written on one is not auto-injected on the other; memsearch still finds it. Durable project facts belong in the repo's `docs/` so both machines see them.

Do not restate the memory procedure in this file. It has one home, and that home is the skill.

---

`AGENTS.md` is the sibling of this file for harnesses that have no Skill tool (Codex and similar). It intentionally carries the memory rules as plain prose instead of routing to a skill. **The two files are not meant to be identical — do not "fix" the difference by symlinking them.**

One line per memory: title, file, and a hook that says when to open it.
